af.about: A landlocked, mountainous country at the crossroads of Central and South Asia, wedged between Iran, Pakistan and the former Soviet republics. About 40 million people speak Dari and Pashto. The modern state dates from the Durrani Empire of 1747; it later served as a buffer in the Anglo-Russian Great Game and won full independence in 1919. A Soviet invasion in 1979 began four decades of war: civil conflict, Taliban rule, a US-led intervention in 2001, and the Taliban's return in 2021. It is now an Islamic emirate under Taliban control.
known: Hindu Kush mountains and Khyber Pass

ax.about: An autonomous and demilitarised archipelago of Finland in the Baltic Sea, between Sweden and the Finnish mainland. Its roughly 30,000 inhabitants are Swedish-speaking and govern themselves through their own parliament, the Lagting, with their own flag and stamps. The islands passed from Sweden to Russia with Finland in 1809 and were demilitarised after the Crimean War. When Finland became independent, Ålanders asked to join Sweden; the League of Nations awarded them to Finland in 1921 with guaranteed autonomy. They joined the EU with Finland in 1995 but stay outside its tax area.
dates: Ceded by Sweden to Russia with Finland
League of Nations grants autonomy under Finland

al.about: A small Balkan country on the Adriatic and Ionian coasts, bordered by Montenegro, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Greece. About 2.8 million people speak Albanian, a language with no close relatives. It is a parliamentary republic, a NATO member and an EU candidate. Descended from the ancient Illyrians, it spent nearly five centuries under Ottoman rule before independence in 1912. After Italian occupation in the Second World War, Enver Hoxha built one of the most isolated communist regimes anywhere, dotting the country with bunkers. Communism collapsed in 1991, followed by a rocky transition.

dz.about: The largest country in Africa, stretching from the Mediterranean deep into the Sahara, which covers most of its territory. About 45 million people live mainly along the coast; Arabic and Berber are official and French is widely used. A presidential republic in which the army is highly influential, it earns most of its income from oil and gas. Home to Numidian kingdoms and Roman cities, it was later an Ottoman regency before France conquered it in 1830 and settled it heavily. A brutal war of independence ended in 1962; a civil war against Islamist insurgents scarred the 1990s.
known: Roman ruins of Timgad and Djémila

as.about: An unincorporated territory of the United States in the South Pacific, comprising the eastern islands of the Samoan archipelago, chiefly Tutuila with its deep harbour at Pago Pago. About 45,000 people speak Samoan and English; they are US nationals rather than citizens and elect their own governor and legislature. Settled by Polynesians some three thousand years ago, Samoa was divided between Germany and the United States in 1899. The US Navy ran the eastern islands until 1951, when civilian administration took over. Traditional chiefly culture, fa'a Samoa, remains strong.
dates: Samoa divided between US and Germany

ad.about: A tiny landlocked principality high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain. About 80,000 people live in its valleys, with Catalan as the official language. Its unusual form of government is a co-principality: the heads of state are the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain, a system dating back to a 1278 treaty, while a constitution adopted in 1993 made it a parliamentary democracy. Long poor and isolated, Andorra prospered in the twentieth century on duty-free shopping, skiing and banking. It is not an EU member but uses the euro.
dates: Consell de la Terra, early parliament, founded
First constitution; joins the United Nations
known: Co-princes: French president and a bishop

ao.about: A large country on the Atlantic coast of south-western Africa, bordered by the two Congos, Zambia and Namibia, with the oil-rich exclave of Cabinda to the north. About 36 million people speak Portuguese and Bantu languages. It is a presidential republic ruled by the MPLA since independence. The Portuguese founded Luanda in 1575 and the colony became a major source of enslaved people for Brazil. Independence in 1975 was followed immediately by a 27-year civil war between the MPLA and UNITA. Since peace in 2002, oil and diamonds have driven growth amid stark inequality.
dates: Independence from Portugal; civil war begins
Civil war ends after Savimbi's death
Dos Santos steps down after 38 years
known: Luanda, once among world's costliest cities

ai.about: A British Overseas Territory in the eastern Caribbean, a flat, dry coral island just north of Saint Martin. Its roughly 15,000 English-speaking inhabitants run their own internal affairs under a UK-appointed governor. Settled by the English in 1650, Anguilla was for centuries administered together with Saint Kitts, an arrangement islanders resented. In 1967 they rebelled, expelled the Kittitian police and declared independence; British paratroopers landed in 1969 and the island was formally separated in 1980. Today it lives on luxury tourism and offshore finance.
dates: Revolt against union with Saint Kitts
British forces land to restore order

ag.about: A twin-island nation in the Leeward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, with most of its roughly 100,000 English-speaking people on Antigua; Barbuda is low, sparsely settled and wildlife-rich. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Colonised by the English in 1632, Antigua became a sugar island worked by enslaved Africans and the base of Britain's Caribbean fleet at Nelson's Dockyard. Independence came in 1981. Tourism now dominates the economy; Hurricane Irma devastated Barbuda in 2017.
known: A beach for every day of the year

ar.about: The second-largest country in South America, running from the subtropical north through the Pampas grasslands to Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego, with the Andes along its border with Chile. About 46 million people speak Spanish; it is a federal presidential republic. A Spanish colony, it declared independence in 1816 and, after civil wars, drew millions of European immigrants to become one of the world's richest countries by 1900. The twentieth century brought Peronism, military dictatorships, the 1976–83 junta's Dirty War and the Falklands defeat. Democracy returned in 1983, punctuated by recurring economic crises.
dates: Military coup begins the Dirty War

am.about: A small, landlocked, mountainous country in the South Caucasus, bordered by Turkey, Georgia, Azerbaijan and Iran. About 3 million people speak Armenian, written in its own alphabet, and a large diaspora lives abroad. It is a parliamentary republic. Armenia was the first state to adopt Christianity, in 301, and its ancient kingdoms were long contested by Persians, Byzantines, Ottomans and Russians. The 1915 genocide in the Ottoman Empire shaped its modern identity. After seven decades as a Soviet republic it became independent in 1991, then fought Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, losing the region in 2020–23.

aw.about: A small, dry island off the coast of Venezuela and a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, which handles its defence and foreign affairs. About 110,000 people speak Papiamento and Dutch, plus English and Spanish. Claimed by Spain in 1499 and taken by the Dutch in 1636, Aruba stayed a quiet backwater until a huge oil refinery opened in the 1920s. In 1986 it left the Netherlands Antilles to gain separate status within the Kingdom, and later shelved plans for full independence. Tourism, helped by its position outside the hurricane belt, now drives the economy.
dates: Separate status within the Dutch Kingdom

au.about: A continent-sized country between the Indian and Pacific oceans, the sixth-largest in the world, with a vast arid interior and a population of about 27 million concentrated in coastal cities. English-speaking, it is a federal parliamentary democracy and a Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Aboriginal peoples have lived here for at least 60,000 years. Britain founded a penal colony at Sydney in 1788; gold rushes brought settlers in the 1850s, and six colonies federated in 1901. Post-war immigration made it multicultural; a 1999 referendum on becoming a republic failed.
known: Sydney Opera House and Harbour Bridge

at.about: A landlocked Alpine country in Central Europe bordering eight countries, including Germany, Italy, Switzerland and Hungary. About 9 million people speak German. It is a federal parliamentary republic, constitutionally neutral since 1955 and an EU member since 1995. For six centuries the Habsburgs ruled from Vienna, heading the Holy Roman Empire and then the vast Austro-Hungarian monarchy, which collapsed in 1918 leaving a small republic. Annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938 and occupied by the Allies after 1945, Austria regained full sovereignty with the State Treaty of 1955 and has since been prosperous and stable.
dates: State Treaty restores independence and neutrality
known: Vienna's palaces, opera and coffee houses
Salzburg and The Sound of Music

az.about: A country in the South Caucasus on the Caspian Sea, bordered by Russia, Georgia, Armenia and Iran, with the exclave of Nakhchivan beyond Armenia. About 10 million people speak Azerbaijani, a Turkic language; most are Shia Muslims in a secular state. It is an authoritarian presidential republic ruled by the Aliyev family since 1993. Russia took the region from Persia in the early 1800s and Baku's oil boom followed. After a brief republic in 1918–20 it was Soviet until 1991. It then lost Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenian forces, but retook the territory in wars of 2020 and 2023.
known: Mud volcanoes and burning hillside Yanar Dag

bs.about: An archipelago of some 700 islands and cays in the Atlantic, south-east of Florida and north of Cuba, with most of its roughly 400,000 English-speaking people on New Providence around Nassau. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here in 1492. English settlers arrived in 1648, pirates such as Blackbeard used the islands as a base until Britain imposed order in 1718, and American Loyalists arrived after 1783. Independence came in 1973; tourism and offshore banking dominate the economy.
dates: Columbus's first landfall in the Americas

bh.about: A small island kingdom in the Persian Gulf, linked to Saudi Arabia by the King Fahd Causeway. About 1.5 million people live here, over half of them foreign workers; Arabic is official. It is a monarchy under the Sunni Al Khalifa dynasty, ruling a majority Shia population, with a parliament of limited power. Site of the ancient Dilmun trading civilisation and later a pearling centre, Bahrain was a British protectorate from the nineteenth century and in 1932 found the Gulf's first oil. It became independent in 1971; Arab Spring protests in 2011 were suppressed with Saudi help. Banking has replaced declining oil.
dates: First oil discovered in the Gulf
known: Tree of Life in the desert

bd.about: One of the world's most densely populated countries, occupying the low delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra on the Bay of Bengal, almost entirely surrounded by India. About 170 million people speak Bengali; it is a parliamentary republic. Part of Mughal and British Bengal, it became East Pakistan at partition in 1947, separated from West Pakistan by 1,600 km of India. Resentment, sharpened by the 1952 language movement, led to a bloody independence war in 1971 won with Indian help. Garment exports have fuelled rapid growth since; floods and cyclones remain constant threats. Mass protests ousted Sheikh Hasina in 2024.
dates: Partition of India; becomes East Pakistan

bb.about: The easternmost island of the Caribbean, a flat coral island of about 280,000 English-speaking people. Settled by the English in 1627 and never ruled by anyone else, it became a hugely profitable sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans and was known as Little England for its British ways. Slavery ended in 1834, independence came in 1966, and in 2021 Barbados removed the British monarch to become a parliamentary republic within the Commonwealth. Today it is one of the region's most prosperous societies, living on tourism, finance and rum.

by.about: A landlocked, flat and forested country in Eastern Europe between Russia, Ukraine, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. About 9 million people; Belarusian and Russian are official, with Russian dominant. It is an authoritarian presidential republic ruled by Alexander Lukashenko since 1994 and closely allied with Russia. Its lands belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and Poland before Russia absorbed them in the late 1700s. The Second World War killed a quarter of the population, and the 1986 Chernobyl disaster contaminated the south. Independent since 1991, it saw mass protests after a disputed 2020 election, which were crushed.
dates: Absorbed by Russia in Poland's partition

be.about: A small, densely populated country in Western Europe between France, the Netherlands, Germany and Luxembourg, with a short North Sea coast. About 11.7 million people are divided between Dutch-speaking Flanders, French-speaking Wallonia and bilingual Brussels, plus a small German community; the language divide shapes its politics. It is a federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy and hosts the headquarters of the EU and NATO. Long a battleground of Europe under Burgundian, Spanish and Austrian rule, it broke from the Netherlands in 1830, ruled the Congo brutally, was overrun in both world wars and co-founded the European project.
dates: German invasion in the First World War
known: Brussels, home of EU and NATO
Cycling classics like Tour of Flanders

bz.about: A small country on the Caribbean coast of Central America, bordered by Mexico and Guatemala, with jungle inland and the hemisphere's largest barrier reef offshore. About 400,000 people; English is official, the only such case in Central America, with Spanish and Kriol widely spoken. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. Once part of the Maya heartland, it was settled by British logwood cutters in the 1600s and became the colony of British Honduras. Renamed Belize in 1973, it gained independence in 1981. Guatemala long claimed its territory; the dispute is now before the International Court of Justice.
dates: Maya city of Caracol at its height
Battle of St George's Caye repels Spain
Hurricane Hattie; capital moved to Belmopan
known: Barrier reef and Great Blue Hole
Maya ruins of Caracol and Xunantunich

bj.about: A narrow West African country on the Gulf of Guinea, between Togo and Nigeria, stretching north to Burkina Faso and Niger. About 13 million people; French is official alongside Fon, Yoruba and others. It is a presidential republic; Porto-Novo is the official capital while government sits in Cotonou. The Kingdom of Dahomey, famous for its female warriors, dominated the coast and the slave trade from the 1600s until France conquered it in 1894. Independent as Dahomey in 1960, it endured coups and a Marxist regime, took the name Benin in 1975, and in 1990 pioneered Africa's wave of democratic transitions.

bm.about: A British Overseas Territory in the North Atlantic about 1,000 km east of the Carolinas, far from the Caribbean despite its tropical image. Some 64,000 people, English-speaking, enjoy one of the world's highest incomes thanks to offshore insurance and reinsurance. Bermuda has had a parliament since 1620, making it Britain's oldest self-governing colony. Uninhabited when sighted by Juan de Bermúdez around 1505, it was settled after the English ship Sea Venture wrecked there in 1609, an event said to have inspired Shakespeare's The Tempest. Voters rejected independence in a 1995 referendum.
dates: Sea Venture wreck brings English settlers

bt.about: A small, landlocked Himalayan kingdom between Tibet and India, rising from subtropical plains to peaks over 7,000 metres. About 800,000 people speak Dzongkha and practise Vajrayana Buddhism. A constitutional monarchy since 2008, it famously measures progress by Gross National Happiness. Unified by a Tibetan lama in the 1600s and ruled by the Wangchuck dynasty since 1907, Bhutan stayed almost sealed off from the world until the 1960s, admitting television and the internet only in 1999. It limits tourism, protects its forests by law and remains one of the few carbon-negative countries.

bo.about: A landlocked country in the heart of South America, from the high Andean altiplano in the west to Amazon lowlands in the east. About 12 million people; Spanish is official alongside Quechua, Aymara and other Indigenous languages. Sucre is the constitutional capital while government sits in La Paz. Heir to Tiwanaku and the Inca, it supplied Spain with Potosí silver, became independent in 1825 and was named after Simón Bolívar. It lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific, saw a 1952 revolution and many coups, and elected its first Indigenous president, Evo Morales, in 2006.
dates: War of the Pacific; loses coastline
known: La Paz, world's highest seat of government

ba.about: A mountainous Balkan country bordered by Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro, with a sliver of Adriatic coast at Neum. About 3.2 million people belong mostly to three groups: Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats, speaking closely related languages. Under the 1995 Dayton Accords it is split into two entities, the Federation and Republika Srpska, with a three-member rotating presidency. A medieval kingdom, it was Ottoman for four centuries, then Austro-Hungarian; the 1914 assassination in Sarajevo triggered the First World War. Its 1992–95 war of independence from Yugoslavia brought siege, ethnic cleansing and the Srebrenica genocide.
dates: Sarajevo assassination sparks First World War
Srebrenica massacre; Dayton Accords end war
known: Mosques, churches and synagogues side by side

bw.about: A landlocked southern African country, mostly covered by the Kalahari, bordered by South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe and Zambia. About 2.5 million people; English is official and Setswana widely spoken. A stable parliamentary republic, it has held free elections since independence and is often cited as an African success story. Tswana chiefs sought British protection in 1885 to fend off Boer and German expansion, creating the Bechuanaland Protectorate. Independence came in 1966 under Seretse Khama; diamonds discovered the next year turned one of the world's poorest countries into an upper-middle-income one. The ruling party lost power peacefully in 2024.

br.about: The giant of South America and the world's fifth-largest country, holding most of the Amazon basin and a 7,500 km Atlantic coast. About 215 million people speak Portuguese; it is a federal presidential republic. Claimed by Portugal in 1500, it grew rich on sugar, gold and coffee and received more enslaved Africans than any other country. The Portuguese court fled here from Napoleon, and in 1822 Brazil became an independent empire; it abolished slavery in 1888, the last in the Americas, and became a republic a year later. A military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985; the 1988 constitution underpins today's democracy.
known: Rio Carnival, samba and bossa nova

vg.about: A British Overseas Territory of about sixty islands in the Caribbean east of Puerto Rico, with most of its roughly 30,000 English-speaking people on Tortola. It governs its own internal affairs under a UK-appointed governor and uses the US dollar. The Dutch planted a settlement in 1648 before England annexed Tortola in 1672 and introduced sugar and slavery. After emancipation the islands languished until the 1960s, when tourism and yachting took off, and a 1984 law made them one of the world's biggest registries of offshore companies. Hurricane Irma caused severe damage in 2017.

bn.about: A tiny, oil-rich sultanate on the north coast of Borneo, split into two parts and surrounded by the Malaysian state of Sarawak. About 450,000 people speak Malay; most are Muslim. It is an absolute monarchy under Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah, on the throne since 1967 and among the world's longest-reigning monarchs. A powerful empire in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries controlling much of Borneo, Brunei dwindled before becoming a British protectorate in 1888. Oil discovered in 1929 brought great wealth. A revolt in 1962 led to emergency rule still in force; independence came in 1984. A strict sharia penal code was introduced in 2014.
known: Sultan's vast Istana Nurul Iman palace

bg.about: A country in south-eastern Europe on the Black Sea, bordered by Romania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece and Turkey and crossed by the Balkan Mountains. About 6.5 million people speak Bulgarian, written in Cyrillic, which was developed here in the ninth century. It is a parliamentary republic, in NATO since 2004 and the EU since 2007, and adopted the euro in 2026. The First Bulgarian Empire of 681 was a medieval great power; five centuries of Ottoman rule ended with liberation in 1878. After fighting on the losing side in both world wars, Bulgaria spent 1946–89 as a loyal Soviet satellite.
known: Rose oil from the Valley of Roses

bf.about: A landlocked country in the West African Sahel, bordered by Mali, Niger, Benin, Togo, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire. About 23 million people; French is official and Mooré the largest local language. Since coups in 2022 it has been run by a military junta that has turned from France toward Russia and left ECOWAS with Mali and Niger, while fighting a jihadist insurgency that controls much of the countryside. The Mossi kingdoms ruled here from medieval times until France created the colony of Upper Volta. Independent in 1960, it was renamed Burkina Faso by the revolutionary Thomas Sankara, who was assassinated in 1987.
dates: French colony of Upper Volta created

bi.about: A small, densely populated and landlocked country in Africa's Great Lakes region, bordered by Rwanda, Tanzania and DR Congo along Lake Tanganyika. About 13 million people speak Kirundi; French and English are also official. A presidential republic, it moved its capital from Bujumbura to Gitega in 2019 and is among the world's poorest countries. A kingdom from the 1600s, it passed from German to Belgian rule as part of Ruanda-Urundi and became independent in 1962. Tensions between the Hutu majority and Tutsi minority produced mass killings in 1972 and a civil war from 1993 to 2005.
known: Claimed southernmost source of the Nile

kh.about: A South-East Asian country on the Gulf of Thailand, bordered by Thailand, Laos and Vietnam and centred on the Mekong and the great Tonlé Sap lake. About 17 million people speak Khmer and are mostly Theravada Buddhist. A constitutional monarchy in form, it has been dominated since the 1980s by Hun Sen's party, with his son Hun Manet prime minister since 2023. The Khmer Empire built Angkor and ruled much of the region from the ninth to fifteenth centuries. A French protectorate from 1863, Cambodia became independent in 1953, then suffered the Khmer Rouge genocide of 1975–79, which killed around two million people.
known: Killing Fields of the Khmer Rouge

cm.about: A Central African country on the Gulf of Guinea, bordered by Nigeria, Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon and Equatorial Guinea. Called Africa in miniature for its range of deserts, mountains, rainforest and coast, it has about 28 million people speaking French, English and over 250 local languages. It is a presidential republic ruled by Paul Biya since 1982. A German colony from 1884, it was split between France and Britain after the First World War; the French part became independent in 1960 and the British south joined it in 1961. Since 2017 an Anglophone separatist conflict has troubled the west.

ca.about: The world's second-largest country by area, spanning North America from the Atlantic to the Pacific and far into the Arctic, though most of its roughly 40 million people live within a short drive of the US border. English and French are official; it is a federal parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm of ten provinces and three territories. Home to Indigenous peoples for millennia, it was colonised by France from 1608 and conquered by Britain in 1763. The colonies confederated in 1867, a transcontinental railway bound them together, and full constitutional independence came in 1982. Quebec twice voted against separation (1980, and very narrowly in 1995).
dates: Confederation creates the Dominion of Canada
Constitution patriated with Charter of Rights
known: Maple syrup and the maple leaf

cv.about: An archipelago of ten volcanic islands in the Atlantic, about 570 km off Senegal. Around 550,000 people live here, speaking Portuguese and the Creole language Kriolu, while an even larger diaspora lives abroad. It is a stable multiparty republic, one of Africa's best-governed. Uninhabited until Portuguese settlers arrived in the 1460s, the islands became a hub of the Atlantic slave trade and later suffered devastating droughts and famines. Independence came in 1975 under the party that also freed Guinea-Bissau; plans to unite the two countries were dropped in 1980. Tourism and remittances sustain the economy.
known: Beaches of Sal and Boa Vista

bq.about: Three small Caribbean islands, Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, that have been special municipalities of the Netherlands since the Netherlands Antilles was dissolved in 2010. Bonaire lies off Venezuela; Statia and Saba are in the Leeward Islands near Sint Maarten. Together they have about 30,000 people; Dutch is official, with Papiamento spoken on Bonaire and English on the other two, and the US dollar is the currency. The Dutch took them in the 1630s. Statia, once a bustling free port, fired the first foreign salute to the American flag in 1776. Bonaire is a diving destination; Saba holds the Kingdom's highest point.
dates: Sint Eustatius salutes the American flag
Become special municipalities of the Netherlands
known: Saba's Mount Scenery, Kingdom's highest peak

ky.about: A British Overseas Territory of three islands in the western Caribbean south of Cuba: Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman. About 80,000 people, English-speaking, enjoy the highest living standard in the Caribbean. It governs itself internally under a UK-appointed governor. Columbus sighted the islands in 1503 and England acquired them with Jamaica in 1670; they were a dependency of Jamaica until it became independent in 1962, when Cayman chose to remain British. From the 1960s a tax-free regime turned it into one of the world's largest financial centres, home to thousands of hedge funds. Hurricane Ivan struck hard in 2004.

cf.about: The Central African Republic is a landlocked country in the heart of Africa, bordered by Chad, Sudan, the two Congos and Cameroon. It has about 5.5 million people, speaks French and Sango, and is nominally a presidential republic. Once the French colony of Ubangi-Shari, it became independent in 1960 and soon fell under Jean-Bédel Bokassa, who crowned himself emperor in 1976. Decades of coups followed, and a 2013 rebellion plunged the country into a civil war that has left it one of the poorest and least stable nations on earth despite rich diamond, gold and timber resources.
dates: Séléka rebels take Bangui; civil war

td.about: Chad is a vast landlocked country in north-central Africa, stretching from the Sahara in the north through the Sahel to Lake Chad in the southwest. About 18 million people live there, speaking French and Arabic alongside many local languages, under a strongly presidential system. Independent from France in 1960, Chad endured decades of civil war and conflict with Libya before Idriss Déby took power in 1990. Oil exports began in 2003. Déby was killed fighting rebels in 2021 and was succeeded by his son, Mahamat Déby.
dates: Déby killed; his son takes over

cl.about: Chile is a ribbon of land running 4,300 km down South America's Pacific coast, squeezed between the Andes and the ocean, from the Atacama Desert to the fjords of Patagonia. Around 20 million people, nearly all Spanish-speaking, live in this presidential republic, a third of them in Santiago. Chile won independence from Spain in 1818 and gained its mineral-rich north in the War of the Pacific. The 1973 coup against Salvador Allende brought Augusto Pinochet's dictatorship, which ended in 1990. Today Chile is one of Latin America's wealthiest and most stable economies, built on copper, wine and fruit.
dates: War of the Pacific; gains the north

cn.about: China fills much of East Asia and, with about 1.4 billion people, is the world's second most populous country and its second-largest economy. Mandarin is the official language; the country is a one-party state ruled by the Communist Party. Chinese civilisation stretches back over three thousand years, and the empire founded by the Qin in 221 BC lasted, through many dynasties, until 1912. After civil war and Japanese invasion, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949. Reforms from 1978 turned China into the workshop of the world and lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty.

cx.about: Christmas Island is an Australian external territory in the Indian Ocean, about 350 km south of Java. The rugged, forested island was named when sighted on Christmas Day 1643, annexed by Britain in 1888 for its phosphate deposits, and transferred from Singapore to Australia in 1958. Fewer than 2,000 people live there, most of Chinese or Malay heritage. Much of the island is national park, and it is famous for the annual migration of millions of red crabs to the sea. It also housed Australia's offshore immigration detention centre.

cc.about: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are two coral atolls in the Indian Ocean, roughly halfway between Australia and Sri Lanka, forming an Australian external territory. About 600 people live on two of the 27 islands, most of them Cocos Malay Muslims descended from plantation workers. Settled in 1827, the islands were ruled for 150 years as a private fief by the Scottish Clunies-Ross family, who were bought out by Australia in 1978. In 1984 the islanders voted to integrate fully with Australia.

co.about: Colombia sits at the northwest corner of South America with coasts on both the Caribbean and the Pacific, spanning Andean mountains, Amazon rainforest and tropical plains. Its roughly 52 million Spanish-speaking people make it the continent's second most populous country, governed as a presidential republic. Liberated from Spain by Simón Bolívar in 1819, it later lost Panama and suffered long bouts of political violence. A guerrilla war with the FARC lasted from 1964 until a 2016 peace accord, and drug cartels shaped its late twentieth century. Today it is known for coffee, music and extraordinary biodiversity.

km.about: The Comoros are a volcanic archipelago in the Mozambique Channel between Madagascar and mainland Africa. Three islands form the Union of the Comoros, home to about 900,000 people who speak Comorian, Arabic and French; the fourth island, Mayotte, voted to remain French. Independent since 1975, the country has suffered more than twenty coups and attempted coups, including several by the mercenary Bob Denard. A 2001 constitution gave each island autonomy to end a secession crisis. Most people are Sunni Muslim and farm ylang-ylang, vanilla and cloves.
dates: Independence from France; Mayotte stays French

ck.about: The Cook Islands are fifteen islands scattered across the South Pacific between French Polynesia and Samoa. Named after Captain James Cook, they became a British protectorate in 1888 and were annexed to New Zealand in 1901. Since 1965 they have been self-governing in free association with New Zealand, which handles defence; Cook Islanders are New Zealand citizens. About 15,000 people live there, mostly on Rarotonga, speaking Cook Islands Māori and English, and many more live in New Zealand. Tourism and black pearls drive the economy.
dates: Self-government in free association with New Zealand

cr.about: Costa Rica is a small Central American republic between Nicaragua and Panama, with coasts on both the Caribbean and the Pacific. About 5 million Spanish-speaking people live in one of Latin America's most stable democracies. Independent from Spain in 1821, it escaped most of the region's upheavals; after a brief civil war in 1948 it abolished its army and invested in education and health instead. A quarter of its territory is protected, and its rainforests, volcanoes and beaches have made it a pioneer of eco-tourism.
dates: President Arias wins Nobel Peace Prize

hr.about: Croatia curves around the Adriatic Sea in southeastern Europe, from the plains around Zagreb to a coast of over a thousand islands. Its roughly 3.9 million people speak Croatian and live in a parliamentary republic. A medieval kingdom from 925, Croatia spent centuries under Hungarian, Venetian and Habsburg rule before joining Yugoslavia in 1918. It declared independence in 1991, fought a four-year war against Serb forces, and joined the EU in 2013, adopting the euro and entering Schengen in 2023. Tourism along the Dalmatian coast dominates the economy.
dates: Adopts the euro and joins Schengen

cu.about: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, lying just 150 km south of Florida. Its roughly 11 million people speak Spanish and live under a one-party communist state. A Spanish colony from 1492 and a major sugar producer, Cuba became independent in 1902 under heavy American influence. Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution turned it into a Soviet ally, provoking the Bay of Pigs invasion and the 1962 Missile Crisis. A US embargo and the Soviet collapse brought lasting hardship, but Cuba is famed for its music, cigars and free health care.
known: Havana's vintage cars and colonial streets

cw.about: Curaçao is a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, an island in the southern Caribbean about 65 km off Venezuela. About 150,000 people live there, speaking Papiamentu, Dutch and English. Captured by the Dutch in 1634, it became a major hub of the Atlantic slave trade and later of oil refining for Venezuelan crude. When the Netherlands Antilles was dissolved in 2010, Curaçao gained autonomy in internal affairs while the Netherlands keeps defence and foreign policy. Tourism, finance and the port drive the economy.
dates: Becomes autonomous country within the Kingdom

cy.about: Cyprus is an island in the eastern Mediterranean, south of Turkey, with about 1.2 million people speaking Greek and Turkish. It is a presidential republic and EU member. Ruled over the centuries by Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Crusaders, Venetians and Ottomans, it passed to Britain in 1878 and became independent in 1960. In 1974 a Greek-backed coup triggered a Turkish invasion, and the island has been divided ever since: the Turkish Cypriot north declared a republic in 1983 recognised only by Turkey, while a UN buffer zone runs through Nicosia, the last divided capital in Europe.
dates: Coup and Turkish invasion; island divided
known: Beaches of Ayia Napa and Paphos

cz.about: Czechia, or the Czech Republic, is a landlocked country in central Europe made up of Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia. Its roughly 10.9 million people speak Czech and live in a parliamentary republic. Prague was the seat of the Holy Roman Empire under Charles IV in the fourteenth century, and the Czech lands later spent four hundred years under the Habsburgs. Czechoslovakia emerged in 1918, fell to Nazi Germany and then to communism, and was freed by the 1989 Velvet Revolution. The peaceful split from Slovakia came in 1993 and EU membership in 2004.
dates: Charles IV begins Prague's golden age
Prague Spring crushed by Soviet tanks

dk.about: Denmark is the southernmost Nordic country, occupying the Jutland peninsula and over 400 islands between the North and Baltic Seas; Greenland and the Faroe Islands are self-governing parts of the realm. About 6 million people speak Danish in a constitutional monarchy and EU member. Home of the Vikings, Denmark once ruled a union with Norway and Sweden, lost Norway in 1814 and Schleswig in 1864, and became a constitutional monarchy in 1849. Today it is a prosperous welfare state renowned for design, wind energy and consistently high rankings for happiness.
dates: Harald Bluetooth unites Denmark and adopts Christianity
Kalmar Union with Norway and Sweden

dj.about: Djibouti is a small, arid country on the Horn of Africa, guarding the Bab-el-Mandeb strait where the Red Sea meets the Gulf of Aden. About 1 million people, mainly Somali and Afar, speak French, Arabic, Somali and Afar under a long-serving president. Formerly French Somaliland, it gained independence in 1977. Its strategic location has drawn military bases from France, the United States, China, Japan and others, and its port handles most of landlocked Ethiopia's trade, linked by a modern railway to Addis Ababa.
dates: China opens its first overseas base
known: Whale sharks in the Gulf of Tadjoura

dm.about: Dominica is a mountainous volcanic island in the eastern Caribbean, between Guadeloupe and Martinique, known as the Nature Isle. About 70,000 people speak English and a French-based creole in this parliamentary republic. The last Caribbean island to be colonised, it passed from France to Britain in 1763 and became independent in 1978. It still has a Kalinago (Carib) reserve, the largest indigenous community in the region. Hurricane Maria devastated the island in 2017. Dominica is not to be confused with the Dominican Republic.
known: Boiling Lake and Morne Trois Pitons

do.about: The Dominican Republic occupies the eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola, the Caribbean island it shares with Haiti. About 11 million Spanish-speaking people live in this presidential republic, whose capital Santo Domingo is the oldest European city in the Americas. The country declared independence from Haitian rule in 1844, endured the brutal Trujillo dictatorship from 1930 to 1961 and a US intervention in 1965, and has since grown into the Caribbean's largest economy. Beach resorts, baseball and merengue define its image abroad.

cd.about: The Democratic Republic of the Congo is Africa's second-largest country, spanning the Congo River basin and the world's second-largest rainforest in the centre of the continent. Around 100 million people speak French plus Lingala, Swahili and hundreds of other languages. Seized by Belgium's King Leopold II as a brutal private domain in 1885, it became the Belgian Congo and gained independence in 1960. Mobutu Sese Seko ruled as dictator for 32 years, renaming the country Zaire. His fall in 1997 led to devastating wars, and conflict continues in the mineral-rich east.
dates: Congo Free State under Leopold II

ec.about: Ecuador straddles the equator on South America's Pacific coast, with the Andes running down its spine and Amazon lowlands to the east. About 18 million people, speaking Spanish and Quechua, live in this presidential republic. Once part of the Inca Empire and then the Spanish Empire, it won independence in 1822 and left Gran Colombia in 1830. It adopted the US dollar in 2000 after a banking collapse. Ecuador is the world's largest banana exporter and governs the Galápagos Islands, whose wildlife inspired Darwin.

eg.about: Egypt lies in the northeast corner of Africa, with the Sinai Peninsula reaching into Asia, and almost all of its roughly 110 million Arabic-speaking people live along the Nile. It is a presidential republic dominated by the military. One of the world's oldest civilisations, pharaonic Egypt was unified around 3100 BC and built the pyramids. It was later ruled by Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Ottomans and Britain. The 1952 revolution brought Nasser and republican rule, Sadat made peace with Israel in 1979, and the 2011 uprising toppled Mubarak.
dates: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt
known: Pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx
Tutankhamun and the Valley of the Kings

sv.about: El Salvador is the smallest and most densely populated country in Central America, lying on the Pacific coast between Guatemala and Honduras. About 6.3 million Spanish-speaking people live in this presidential republic. Independent from Spain in 1821, it was long dominated by coffee oligarchs and the military, and a civil war from 1980 to 1992 killed some 75,000 people. Gang violence followed, until President Nayib Bukele's sweeping crackdown from 2022. In 2021 it became the first country to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender.
dates: Bukele's state of emergency against gangs

gq.about: Equatorial Guinea is a small country on the Gulf of Guinea made up of the mainland region of Río Muni and several islands, including Bioko, where Malabo stands. It is Africa's only Spanish-speaking country, with about 1.7 million people and a presidential system that is in practice authoritarian. Independent from Spain in 1968, it suffered the murderous rule of Francisco Macías Nguema until his nephew Teodoro Obiang seized power in 1979; Obiang remains the world's longest-serving president. Oil discovered in the 1990s made it rich on paper, though most citizens stay poor.

er.about: Eritrea stretches along the Red Sea coast of the Horn of Africa, north of Ethiopia. Its few million people speak Tigrinya, Arabic and other languages, and live under one of the world's most closed one-party regimes, led by Isaias Afwerki since independence. An Italian colony from 1890, it was federated with and then annexed by Ethiopia, triggering a thirty-year war of independence that ended in 1993. A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 was followed by a formal peace in 2018. Indefinite national service drives many young Eritreans to emigrate.
known: Dahlak Islands in the Red Sea

ee.about: Estonia is the northernmost of the three Baltic states, facing Finland across the Gulf of Finland. Its 1.3 million people speak Estonian, a Finnic language unrelated to its Latvian and Russian neighbours, and live in a parliamentary republic in the EU and NATO. Ruled in turn by Danes, Germans, Swedes and Russians, Estonia first became independent in 1918, was occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940, and regained freedom in 1991 after the Singing Revolution. It has since become a pioneer of digital government and tech startups.

sz.about: Eswatini, known as Swaziland until 2018, is a small landlocked kingdom in southern Africa wedged between South Africa and Mozambique. About 1.2 million people speak Swazi and English under King Mswati III, Africa's last absolute monarch, who has reigned since 1986. The Swazi kingdom was founded in the eighteenth century, became a British protectorate after the Boer War and gained independence in 1968. The king suspended the constitution and banned political parties in 1973. Sugar, forestry and tourism support an economy heavily tied to South Africa.

et.about: Ethiopia is a landlocked country in the Horn of Africa and, with about 120 million people, the continent's second most populous. It is a federal republic organised along ethnic lines, with Amharic as the working language alongside Oromo and dozens of others. Home to the ancient kingdom of Aksum and one of the world's oldest Christian traditions, Ethiopia famously defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896 and was never colonised. Emperor Haile Selassie was overthrown by the Marxist Derg in 1974; a rebel coalition took power in 1991. A civil war in Tigray raged from 2020 to 2022.
dates: Haile Selassie overthrown by the Derg

fk.about: The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, about 500 km east of Argentina, which claims them as the Malvinas. Around 3,500 people live on the two main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, most in Stanley. Britain established permanent rule in 1833. Argentina invaded in 1982, prompting a ten-week war that Britain won. In a 2013 referendum, islanders voted almost unanimously to remain British. Sheep farming, squid fishing licences and tourism sustain a small but prosperous economy.

fo.about: The Faroe Islands are eighteen rugged islands in the North Atlantic between Iceland and Norway, a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. About 54,000 people speak Faroese, a descendant of Old Norse. Settled by Vikings in the ninth century, the islands passed with Norway to the Danish crown and have had home rule since 1948; they are not part of the EU. Fishing and fish farming dominate the economy, and the islands' sea cliffs, grass-roofed houses and dramatic weather draw growing numbers of visitors.

fj.about: Fiji is an archipelago of over 300 islands in the South Pacific, about 2,000 km north of New Zealand. Its roughly 900,000 people are mostly indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians, descendants of indentured labourers brought by the British, and speak Fijian, Hindi and English. A British colony from 1874, Fiji became independent in 1970 but has since seen four coups, driven largely by ethnic tensions. It is a parliamentary republic. Tourism, sugar and remittances support the economy, and rugby is a national passion.

fi.about: Finland is a Nordic country of forests and some 188,000 lakes, lying between Sweden and Russia and stretching north into Lapland. Its 5.6 million people speak Finnish and Swedish and live in a parliamentary republic that joined the EU in 1995 and NATO in 2023. Part of Sweden for six centuries and a Russian grand duchy from 1809, Finland declared independence in 1917 and held off a Soviet invasion in the Winter War. It became a prosperous welfare state and regularly tops global happiness rankings.
dates: Winter War against the Soviet Union

fr.about: France is the largest country in Western Europe, stretching from the Channel and the Atlantic to the Mediterranean and the Alps, with overseas territories around the globe. About 68 million people speak French in a semi-presidential republic that is a founding member of the EU and a nuclear power. Rome's Gaul became the kingdom of the Franks, and medieval and absolutist France grew into a great power. The 1789 Revolution overthrew the monarchy, Napoleon conquered much of Europe, and after empires and republics the present Fifth Republic was founded in 1958.
dates: Treaty of Verdun creates West Francia

pf.about: French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France made up of 118 islands spread across the South Pacific, including Tahiti, Moorea and Bora Bora. About 280,000 people speak French and Tahitian; the territory has broad internal autonomy, while France handles defence and currency. Tahiti became a French protectorate in 1842 and a colony in 1880. From 1966 to 1996 France carried out nuclear tests at Mururoa and Fangataufa atolls. Tourism, black pearls and French subsidies support the economy.
known: Bora Bora's lagoon and overwater bungalows

ga.about: Gabon lies on the equator on Africa's Atlantic coast, with nearly 90 percent of its land covered by rainforest. About 2.4 million people speak French and Bantu languages in one of Africa's wealthier countries, thanks to oil, manganese and timber. Independent from France in 1960, it was ruled for over half a century by the Bongo family: Omar Bongo from 1967 and his son Ali from 2009, until a military coup in 2023. Gabon is a leader in forest conservation, with thirteen national parks.

gm.about: The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa, a narrow strip along the Gambia River entirely surrounded by Senegal except for its Atlantic coast. About 2.7 million people speak English, Mandinka, Wolof and other languages in a presidential republic. A British colony built around the river trade, it became independent in 1965. Yahya Jammeh ruled harshly from a 1994 coup until he was forced out in 2017 after losing an election. Peanuts, tourism and remittances support the economy.
dates: Jammeh forced out after election defeat
known: Kunta Kinte and the novel Roots

ge.about: Georgia lies in the Caucasus at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, between the Black Sea and the mountains bordering Russia. Its roughly 3.7 million people speak Georgian, with its own unique alphabet, and live in a parliamentary republic. One of the first countries to adopt Christianity, Georgia had a medieval golden age before falling under Persian, Ottoman and then Russian rule in 1801. Independent briefly in 1918, it was absorbed by the Soviet Union and regained independence in 1991. Russia backs the breakaway regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, over which the two fought a short war in 2008.

de.about: Germany lies at the heart of Europe, from the North Sea and Baltic coasts to the Alps, and is the EU's most populous country and largest economy, with about 84 million German-speaking people in a federal parliamentary republic. Fragmented for centuries within the Holy Roman Empire, Germany was unified under Prussia in 1871. Defeat in the First World War, the Weimar Republic and the Nazi dictatorship led to the Second World War and the Holocaust. Divided between West and East during the Cold War, Germany reunified in 1990 and is a pillar of the EU.
dates: Otto I crowned Holy Roman Emperor
Divided into West and East Germany

gh.about: Ghana sits on West Africa's Gulf of Guinea coast, between Côte d'Ivoire and Togo. About 33 million people speak English alongside Akan, Ewe and other languages in one of Africa's most stable democracies. The region was home to the powerful Ashanti Empire and, as the Gold Coast, became a hub of the Atlantic slave trade. In 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah it became the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence, inspiring the rest of the continent. After decades of coups, multiparty democracy returned in 1992. Gold, cocoa and oil anchor the economy.
dates: First sub-Saharan colony to gain independence
known: Cape Coast and Elmina slave castles

gi.about: Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory at the southern tip of Spain, a 6-square-kilometre promontory dominated by the Rock, guarding the strait between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. About 34,000 people speak English and Spanish and govern their own affairs, with Britain responsible for defence and foreign policy. Captured by an Anglo-Dutch force in 1704 and ceded to Britain in 1713, it remains claimed by Spain, which closed the land border from 1969 to 1985. Gibraltarians voted overwhelmingly to stay British in 1967 and 2002. Finance, online gaming and shipping drive the economy.
dates: Ceded to Britain by Treaty of Utrecht
Referendum rejects shared sovereignty with Spain
known: Barbary macaques, Europe's only wild monkeys

gr.about: Greece sits at the southern tip of the Balkans, a mountainous mainland fringed by thousands of islands in the Aegean and Ionian seas. About 10 million people speak Greek in a parliamentary republic. Its ancient city-states invented democracy, philosophy and the Olympics; Alexander spread Greek culture across the Near East before Rome and then Byzantium absorbed it. Nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule ended with the war of independence in the 1820s. A turbulent 20th century brought monarchy, civil war and a military junta before stable democracy, EU membership and a painful debt crisis in the 2010s.
known: Islands such as Santorini and Crete

gl.about: Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark and the world's largest island, lying between the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans. An ice sheet covers about four fifths of it, so its roughly 57,000 people, mostly Inuit, live in coastal towns and speak Greenlandic and Danish. Norse settlers arrived around 986 and vanished by the 15th century; Danish colonisation began in 1721. Greenland became an integral part of Denmark in 1953, won home rule in 1979, left the European Community in 1985 and gained expanded self-government in 2009. Denmark still handles defence and foreign affairs.
dates: Erik the Red founds Norse settlements
Becomes part of the Kingdom of Denmark

gd.about: Grenada is a small volcanic island nation at the southern end of the Caribbean's Windward Islands, with about 125,000 English-speaking people. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm with the British monarch as head of state. Colonised by the French in the 17th century and ceded to Britain in 1763, it became independent in 1974. A 1979 left-wing revolution ended in 1983 when its leader was killed in an internal coup, prompting a US-led invasion. Nicknamed the Spice Isle, it is a major producer of nutmeg and mace and relies heavily on tourism.
dates: Revolution brings Maurice Bishop to power
known: Nutmeg and the Spice Isle nickname

gu.about: Guam is an unincorporated territory of the United States, the largest and southernmost of the Mariana Islands in the western Pacific. Its roughly 170,000 people, including the indigenous Chamorro, are US citizens who speak English and Chamorro but cannot vote for president. Spain claimed the island after Magellan's 1521 visit and ruled it until ceding it to the United States in 1898. Japan occupied Guam during the Second World War before US forces retook it in 1944. The 1950 Organic Act granted civilian government, and large US naval and air bases remain central to the economy alongside tourism.

gt.about: Guatemala is the most populous country in Central America, with about 18 million people, lying south of Mexico between the Pacific and the Caribbean. Spanish is official but over twenty Mayan languages are spoken, and nearly half the population is indigenous. The heartland of ancient Maya civilisation, it was conquered by Spain in 1524 and became independent in 1821. A US-backed coup in 1954 toppled a reformist government and helped trigger a 36-year civil war that killed some 200,000 people, mostly Maya. Peace accords in 1996 restored civilian democracy, though poverty and corruption persist.
dates: Peace accords end the civil war

gg.about: Guernsey is a British Crown Dependency in the Channel Islands, close to the Normandy coast of France. It is not part of the United Kingdom or the EU: it governs itself through the States of Guernsey while the UK handles defence and foreign affairs. About 64,000 people live there, speaking English, with a fading Norman French dialect. Part of the Duchy of Normandy when William conquered England in 1066, it stayed loyal to the English crown after Normandy was lost in 1204. German forces occupied the island from 1940 to 1945. Finance is the main industry alongside tourism.
dates: Part of Normandy under William the Conqueror
known: Castle Cornet and St Peter Port harbour

gn.about: Guinea lies on the Atlantic coast of West Africa, with about 14 million people. French is the official language alongside Fula, Malinke and Susu, and most people are Muslim. It is a presidential republic with a history of coups. Once part of the Mali Empire, it became a French colony in the 1890s and in 1958 was the only French territory to vote for immediate independence. Sékou Touré ruled as a one-party dictator until 1984, followed by Lansana Conté until 2008 and further military takeovers, most recently in 2021. Guinea holds the world's largest bauxite reserves.
dates: Military coup after Sékou Touré's death

gw.about: Guinea-Bissau is a small, low-lying country on the West African coast between Senegal and Guinea, including the Bijagós archipelago. About 2 million people speak Portuguese officially and Crioulo in daily life. Formerly part of the Kaabu kingdom and then a Portuguese colony, it fought a guerrilla war from 1963 under Amílcar Cabral and won independence in 1974. Since then it has suffered repeated coups, a civil war in 1998 and 1999, and chronic instability; no elected president completed a full term until 2014. It is one of the world's poorest countries, dependent on cashew nuts.
dates: Coup brings João Vieira to power

gy.about: Guyana sits on the northeast coast of South America, the continent's only English-speaking country, with about 800,000 people of mostly Indian and African descent. Dense rainforest covers most of the interior while almost everyone lives on the coastal plain. Dutch colonies passed to Britain in 1814 and became British Guiana; independence came in 1966 and a republic in 1970. Politics has long split along ethnic lines. Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, two thirds of the country. Vast offshore oil finds since 2015 have made Guyana one of the world's fastest-growing economies.

ht.about: Haiti occupies the western third of Hispaniola in the Caribbean, with about 11.5 million people speaking Haitian Creole and French. As the French colony of Saint-Domingue it was the richest sugar colony in the world, worked by enslaved Africans. Their revolt from 1791 produced in 1804 the first independent Black republic and the only successful slave revolution. Crippling reparations to France, US occupation, the Duvalier dictatorships and repeated coups left it the poorest country in the Americas. A 2010 earthquake killed well over 100,000 people, and since the 2021 assassination of the president gangs have controlled much of the capital.

hn.about: Honduras lies in the middle of Central America with a long Caribbean coast and a short Pacific one, home to about 10.5 million Spanish-speaking people. The Maya city of Copán flourished here before Spanish conquest in the 1520s. Independent from 1821 and briefly part of a Central American federation, it became the archetypal banana republic in the 20th century, dominated by US fruit companies. It fought the brief Football War with El Salvador in 1969, was devastated by Hurricane Mitch in 1998, and saw a coup in 2009. Gang violence and poverty drive heavy emigration.

hk.about: Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of China on the south coast, a dense city of about 7.5 million people speaking Cantonese and English. Britain took Hong Kong Island after the First Opium War in 1842, added Kowloon in 1860 and leased the New Territories for 99 years in 1898. It grew into a global financial hub and returned to China in 1997 under the one country, two systems principle, keeping its own legal system, currency and freedoms for 50 years. Mass protests in 2019 were followed by a 2020 national security law that sharply curtailed political dissent.
dates: Ceded to Britain after the Opium War
known: Dim sum and cha chaan teng cafés
Kung fu cinema and Bruce Lee

hu.about: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe on the Danube plain, with about 9.6 million people speaking Hungarian, a Uralic language unrelated to its neighbours. It is a parliamentary republic and EU member. Magyar tribes settled the Carpathian Basin in 895 and Stephen I founded a Christian kingdom in 1000. Ottoman defeat at Mohács split the kingdom, Habsburg rule followed, and the 1867 compromise created Austria-Hungary. The 1920 Treaty of Trianon stripped two thirds of its territory. Soviet tanks crushed the 1956 uprising; communism ended in 1989, and the country joined the EU in 2004.

is.about: Iceland is a volcanic island nation in the North Atlantic just below the Arctic Circle, with about 390,000 people speaking Icelandic, a language close to Old Norse. It is a parliamentary republic. Norse settlers arrived around 874 and in 930 founded the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments. Iceland came under Norwegian and then Danish rule for centuries, gained sovereignty in 1918 and became a fully independent republic in 1944. Fishing, geothermal and hydro power, and tourism drive the economy, which collapsed spectacularly in the 2008 banking crisis before recovering.
dates: Becomes a sovereign state under Denmark

in.about: India occupies most of the South Asian subcontinent, stretching from the Himalayas to the Indian Ocean. With about 1.4 billion people it is the world's most populous country and its largest democracy, a federal parliamentary republic with Hindi, English and twenty other official languages. Civilisation here dates to the Indus Valley around 2500 BC; empires such as the Maurya, Gupta and Mughal followed. Britain ruled directly from 1858 until 1947, when independence came with the traumatic partition that created Pakistan. Economic liberalisation after 1991 turned it into a major technology and services power.

id.about: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelago, some 17,000 islands stretching along the equator between the Indian and Pacific oceans. With about 280 million people it is the fourth most populous country and the largest Muslim-majority one, united by the Indonesian language in a presidential republic. Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms such as Srivijaya and Majapahit preceded Islam; the Dutch dominated from the 17th century as the Dutch East Indies. Independence was proclaimed in 1945 after Japanese occupation and recognised in 1949. Suharto's authoritarian New Order lasted from the mid-1960s until 1998, when democracy returned.
dates: Mass killings bring Suharto to power
known: Volcanoes along the Ring of Fire

ir.about: Iran, historically Persia, is a large, mountainous country in western Asia between the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf, with about 89 million people speaking Persian. It is an Islamic republic in which an unelected Supreme Leader holds ultimate power. Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire around 550 BC, and Persian empires rose and fell for over a millennium before the Arab conquest brought Islam. The Safavids made Shia Islam the state religion in 1501. The 1979 revolution overthrew the Shah, and a devastating war with Iraq, sanctions and nuclear tensions have defined the decades since.

iq.about: Iraq lies in western Asia around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, the ancient Mesopotamia where writing, cities and law codes first appeared. About 45 million people speak Arabic and Kurdish; most are Shia Muslims, with large Sunni Arab and Kurdish minorities. Baghdad was the glittering Abbasid capital from 762 until the Mongols sacked it in 1258. After Ottoman rule and a British mandate, a kingdom was founded in 1932 and overthrown in 1958. Saddam Hussein's dictatorship brought wars with Iran and Kuwait, the 2003 US-led invasion toppled him, and years of insurgency and the rise of ISIS followed.

ie.about: Ireland occupies most of an island on the western edge of Europe, with about 5.2 million people speaking English and, in some areas, Irish. It is a parliamentary republic and EU member; Northern Ireland remains part of the United Kingdom. Celtic and Christian from early times, it fell under English control from the 12th century and was absorbed into the United Kingdom in 1801. The Great Famine of the 1840s killed a million and sent millions more abroad. The 1916 Easter Rising led to the Irish Free State in 1922 and a republic in 1949. The 1998 Good Friday Agreement brought peace to the north.
dates: Act of Union with Great Britain
known: Cliffs of Moher and green landscapes

im.about: The Isle of Man is a British Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea between England and Ireland. It is self-governing and not part of the United Kingdom or the EU; the UK handles defence and foreign affairs. About 85,000 people live there, speaking English, with the Manx Gaelic language revived in recent decades. Its parliament, Tynwald, dates from Norse rule over a thousand years ago and claims to be the oldest in continuous existence. The island passed from Norway to Scotland and England, and the British crown bought out its lords in 1765. Offshore finance and e-gaming now dominate the economy.
dates: Norway cedes the island to Scotland
Stanley family become Lords of Man

il.about: Israel is a small country on the eastern Mediterranean, with about 9.9 million people, mostly Jewish with a large Arab minority, speaking Hebrew and Arabic. It is a parliamentary democracy with a strong technology economy. The Zionist movement sought a Jewish homeland from the 1890s; Britain's Balfour Declaration and the Palestine mandate followed. Israel declared independence in 1948 and was immediately at war with its Arab neighbours, and it captured the West Bank, Gaza, Golan and Sinai in 1967. Jerusalem is claimed as capital by both Israel and the Palestinians, and the conflict with the Palestinians remains unresolved.

it.about: Italy is a boot-shaped peninsula reaching into the Mediterranean from the Alps, plus Sicily and Sardinia, with about 59 million Italian-speaking people in a parliamentary republic. Rome ruled an empire spanning the ancient world; after its fall the peninsula split into city-states, kingdoms and papal lands that produced the Renaissance. Italy was unified in 1861 and gained Rome as capital in 1871. Mussolini's fascist regime led it into the Second World War; voters chose a republic in 1946 and Italy helped found the European Community. It remains a global centre of art, design, fashion and food.

ci.about: Ivory Coast, officially Côte d'Ivoire, lies on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, with about 30 million people. French is official among some sixty local languages. Abidjan is the economic capital while Yamoussoukro, birthplace of first president Félix Houphouët-Boigny, became the official capital in 1983. A French colony from 1893, it gained independence in 1960 and prospered under Houphouët-Boigny's long rule as the world's largest cocoa producer. After his death in 1993 came a coup, a north-south civil war and a disputed 2010 election that ended in fighting; stability and growth have since returned.
known: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace

jm.about: Jamaica is the third-largest Caribbean island, south of Cuba, with about 2.8 million people speaking English and Jamaican Patois. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. The Taíno lived here before Spain claimed it in 1494; England seized it in 1655 and built a sugar economy on slavery, which was abolished in the 1830s. Independence came in 1962. Despite its size, Jamaica's cultural reach is enormous: reggae and Bob Marley, Rastafari, dancehall, and sprinters like Usain Bolt. Tourism, bauxite and remittances sustain an economy troubled by debt and violent crime.
dates: Columbus claims the island for Spain

jp.about: Japan is an archipelago of four main islands and thousands of smaller ones off the east coast of Asia, with about 124 million people speaking Japanese. It is a constitutional monarchy with the world's oldest hereditary monarchy and a parliamentary government. Imperial courts at Nara and Kyoto gave way to centuries of samurai rule under shoguns, with the Tokugawa closing the country to the outside world from the 1630s. The 1868 Meiji Restoration launched rapid modernisation and imperial expansion that ended in defeat in 1945. Postwar Japan became a pacifist democracy and the world's second-largest economy by the 1980s.

je.about: Jersey is the largest of the Channel Islands and a British Crown Dependency, lying just off the coast of Normandy. Self-governing through its States Assembly, it is not part of the United Kingdom or the EU; the UK is responsible for defence and foreign relations. About 105,000 people live there, speaking English, with the Norman French dialect Jèrriais surviving among a few. Part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933, it stayed with the English crown when Normandy was lost in 1204. German troops occupied it from 1940 to 1945. Finance dominates the economy, with Jersey Royal potatoes, dairy cattle and tourism alongside.
dates: Becomes part of the Duchy of Normandy
Remains loyal to the English crown

jo.about: Jordan is a mostly desert country in the Middle East, landlocked except for a short Red Sea coast at Aqaba, with about 11 million Arabic-speaking people including millions of Palestinian and Syrian refugees. It is a constitutional monarchy ruled by the Hashemite dynasty, which claims descent from the Prophet Muhammad. Home to the Nabataean city of Petra, the land was long an Ottoman backwater before Britain created the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921. Independent since 1946, Jordan annexed the West Bank in 1950 and lost it to Israel in 1967, then signed peace with Israel in 1994. It is a stable Western ally in a volatile region.
dates: Loses the West Bank in Six-Day War

kz.about: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country and ninth largest overall, stretching across Central Asian steppe from the Caspian Sea to China. About 20 million people speak Kazakh and Russian in a presidential republic dominated for three decades by Nursultan Nazarbayev. Nomadic Kazakh khanates emerged in the 15th century before Russian conquest in the 18th and 19th centuries; Soviet collectivisation caused a devastating famine in the 1930s. Independent since 1991, it moved its capital from Almaty to Astana in 1997 and grew rich on oil, gas and uranium. Russia's Baikonur Cosmodrome still launches rockets from its steppe.

ke.about: Kenya straddles the equator on the east coast of Africa, from Indian Ocean beaches through highlands and the Rift Valley to Lake Victoria. About 55 million people from over forty ethnic groups speak Swahili and English in a presidential republic. Swahili trading cities lined the coast for centuries before Britain made it a protectorate in 1895 and a settler colony. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s hastened independence in 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta; Daniel arap Moi ruled for 24 years. Deadly post-election violence in 2007 led to a new constitution in 2010. Kenya is East Africa's economic hub and a safari destination.
known: Mount Kenya and the Rift Valley

ki.about: Kiribati is a Pacific island nation of 33 coral atolls scattered across an ocean area the size of India, straddling the equator and spanning three island groups. About 130,000 people speak Gilbertese and English in a parliamentary republic. Britain made the Gilbert Islands a protectorate in 1892; the 1943 Battle of Tarawa was among the bloodiest of the Pacific war. Independence came in 1979. In 1995 Kiribati shifted the date line so the whole country shares one day, making it the first to see each new year. With most land barely two metres above sea level, it is among the countries most threatened by rising seas.
dates: Gilbert Islands become a British protectorate
known: First country to see the new year
Low-lying atolls threatened by sea rise

xk.about: Kosovo is a small landlocked country in the Balkans, with about 1.7 million people, overwhelmingly ethnic Albanian with a Serb minority, speaking Albanian and Serbian in a parliamentary republic. Medieval Serbian kingdoms and the 1389 Battle of Kosovo give it deep significance for Serbs; centuries of Ottoman rule followed before Serbia took it in 1912. It was an autonomous province of Yugoslavia until Milošević revoked that status in 1989. A 1998-99 war ended with NATO bombing and UN administration. Kosovo declared independence in 2008; it is recognised by around 100 countries but not by Serbia, Russia or China, and its status remains disputed.
dates: Battle of Kosovo against the Ottomans
Serbia takes Kosovo from the Ottomans
known: Pop stars Dua Lipa and Rita Ora's heritage

kw.about: Kuwait is a small, flat desert state at the head of the Persian Gulf, wedged between Iraq and Saudi Arabia. About 4.5 million people live there, but only around a third are citizens; the rest are foreign workers. Arabic is official and the country is an emirate ruled by the Al-Sabah family since the 18th century, with an elected parliament that is unusually assertive for the Gulf. A British protectorate from 1899, it became independent in 1961. Oil, discovered in 1938, made it among the world's richest countries per head. Iraq's 1990 invasion was reversed by a US-led coalition in the 1991 Gulf War.

kg.about: Kyrgyzstan is a landlocked, overwhelmingly mountainous country in Central Asia, dominated by the Tian Shan range and the vast alpine Lake Issyk-Kul. About 7 million people speak Kyrgyz and Russian in a parliamentary-presidential republic, the most politically open in the region though prone to upheaval. Nomadic Kyrgyz tribes came under Russian rule in the 1870s and became a Soviet republic in 1936. Since independence in 1991, popular uprisings toppled presidents in 2005 and 2010. Gold mining, remittances and herding sustain a poor economy; yurts, horses and the Manas epic poem anchor national identity.

la.about: Laos is a landlocked, mountainous country in Southeast Asia along the Mekong River, with about 7.6 million people speaking Lao. It is one of the world's few remaining one-party communist states. The kingdom of Lan Xang, the Land of a Million Elephants, was founded in 1353; the French made Laos a protectorate in 1893. Independent from 1953, it was engulfed by the Vietnam War, becoming the most heavily bombed country per person in history, with unexploded ordnance still a danger. The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975. Hydropower, mining and tourism to temple-filled Luang Prabang drive a growing economy.

lv.about: Latvia is a flat, forested country on the Baltic Sea between Estonia and Lithuania, with about 1.9 million people speaking Latvian and a large Russian-speaking minority. It is a parliamentary republic and member of the EU and NATO. German crusaders founded Riga in 1201 and ruled through the Livonian Order; Poland, Sweden and then Russia from 1721 followed. Latvia declared independence in 1918, was annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940, and regained freedom in 1991 after the peaceful Singing Revolution and the Baltic Way human chain. It joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014.

lb.about: Lebanon is a small, mountainous country on the eastern Mediterranean, bordered by Syria and Israel, with about 5.5 million people speaking Arabic, plus French and English. It has an unusual power-sharing system dividing top offices among Christians, Sunnis and Shia. Phoenician cities such as Tyre and Byblos traded across the ancient world. After Ottoman rule and a French mandate, independence came in 1943. A civil war from 1975 to 1990 drew in Syria, Israel and the Palestinians, and Hezbollah fought Israel in 2006. Since 2019 a catastrophic financial collapse and the 2020 Beirut port explosion have deepened the crisis.
known: Phoenician heritage of Byblos and Tyre

ls.about: Lesotho is a small, mountainous kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, the only country in the world lying wholly above 1,000 metres. About 2.3 million people speak Sesotho and English in a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary government. King Moshoeshoe I united the Basotho in the 1820s and sought British protection in 1868 to fend off Boer settlers; the colony of Basutoland became independent in 1966. Politics has been marked by coups and disputed elections. Water sold to South Africa, diamonds, textiles and remittances from miners support a poor economy, and HIV rates are among the world's highest.
known: Pony trekking in the Maloti mountains

lr.about: Liberia lies on the Atlantic coast of West Africa between Sierra Leone and Ivory Coast, with about 5.5 million people speaking English and many local languages. Africa's oldest republic, it was founded by freed Black Americans resettled from 1822 by the American Colonization Society and declared independence in 1847. The settler elite dominated until a 1980 coup by Samuel Doe, and two civil wars between 1989 and 2003 killed around 250,000 people. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected female head of state in 2006, and footballer George Weah succeeded her in 2018. Rubber, iron ore and ship registration anchor the economy.
dates: Samuel Doe seizes power in coup

ly.about: Libya is a large, mostly Saharan country on North Africa's Mediterranean coast, with about 7 million Arabic-speaking people clustered along the shore. Greeks, Romans and Phoenicians left spectacular ruins at Cyrene, Leptis Magna and Sabratha. Ottoman rule gave way to brutal Italian colonisation in 1911 and independence as a kingdom in 1951. Muammar Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled eccentrically for 42 years on oil wealth until the 2011 uprising and NATO intervention ended with his death. Rival governments in the east and west have fought intermittently since 2014, and the country remains divided and unstable.

li.about: Liechtenstein is a tiny Alpine principality wedged between Switzerland and Austria along the Rhine, one of only two doubly landlocked countries. About 40,000 German-speaking people live there under a constitutional monarchy in which the prince retains unusually strong powers, confirmed by a 2003 referendum. The Liechtenstein family bought the territory and had it made a principality of the Holy Roman Empire in 1719; it became sovereign in 1806. It abolished its army in 1868, entered a customs union with Switzerland in 1923 and uses the Swiss franc. Banking, precision manufacturing and low taxes make it one of the richest countries per head.
dates: Becomes a principality of the Holy Roman Empire
known: Vaduz Castle, home of the prince
Dental products maker Ivoclar and Hilti tools

lt.about: Lithuania is the southernmost of the three Baltic states, on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea between Latvia, Belarus, Poland and Russia's Kaliningrad exclave. It is a small, flat, forested country of about 2.9 million people, speaking Lithuanian, one of the most archaic living Indo-European languages, and governed as a parliamentary republic. In the Middle Ages the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was one of Europe's largest states, later joined with Poland in a commonwealth. Partitioned by Russia in 1795, it declared independence in 1918, was annexed by the Soviet Union in 1940, and was the first Soviet republic to break away in 1990.
dates: First Soviet republic to declare independence

lu.about: Luxembourg is a small landlocked grand duchy in western Europe, wedged between Belgium, France and Germany. With about 670,000 people, nearly half of them foreign nationals, it is officially trilingual in Luxembourgish, French and German and is ruled as a constitutional monarchy under a grand duke. A fortress city founded in 963, it passed through Burgundian, Spanish, French, Austrian and Dutch hands before becoming fully independent in the nineteenth century. A founding member of the EU and home to several of its institutions, it has transformed from a steel economy into one of the world's richest countries, built on banking and finance.
dates: Schengen Agreement signed on its soil
known: Seat of EU Court of Justice

mo.about: Macau is a special administrative region of China on the Pearl River Delta, across the estuary from Hong Kong. It is a tiny, densely packed territory of about 700,000 people, with Cantonese and Portuguese as official languages. Settled by the Portuguese in the 1550s as a trading post, it was Europe's oldest colony in Asia until it was handed back to China in 1999 under a 'one country, two systems' arrangement that preserves its own legal system and currency until 2049. Today it is the world's biggest gambling centre, with casino revenues far exceeding those of Las Vegas.
dates: Casino monopoly ended, gaming boom begins

mg.about: Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island, lying in the Indian Ocean off the southeast coast of Africa. Its roughly 30 million people speak Malagasy and French and descend from both Southeast Asian seafarers and African migrants. Separated from other landmasses for tens of millions of years, it evolved a unique ecosystem in which most species, including all lemurs, exist nowhere else.
