The Merina kingdom unified much of the island in the nineteenth century before France annexed it in 1896. Independent since 1960, it is a republic that has suffered repeated political crises and remains one of the poorest countries in the world.
dates: Merina kingdom unifies much of island

mw.about: Malawi is a small, landlocked country in southeastern Africa, stretched along the western shore of Lake Malawi, which covers about a fifth of its territory. It has about 21 million people, mostly farmers, speaking Chichewa and English, and is a presidential republic. Scottish missionaries following David Livingstone arrived in the 1870s, and Britain made it the protectorate of Nyasaland in 1891. Independent in 1964, it was ruled for thirty years by the autocratic Hastings Banda before multiparty democracy returned in 1994. Known as the 'Warm Heart of Africa', it is peaceful but among the world's poorest nations.
known: Lake Malawi and its cichlid fish

my.about: Malaysia is a Southeast Asian country split into two parts: Peninsular Malaysia south of Thailand, and the states of Sabah and Sarawak on northern Borneo. It has about 34 million people, a mix of Malays, Chinese and Indians, with Malay the official language and English widely used. It is a federal constitutional monarchy whose king is elected every five years from among the state sultans. Malacca was a great fifteenth-century trading sultanate before Portuguese, Dutch and finally British rule. Independent since 1957 and expanded in 1963, it has grown into an industrialised, upper-middle-income economy and a major exporter of electronics and palm oil.
dates: Malaysia formed with Sabah, Sarawak, Singapore
known: Street food: laksa, nasi lemak, satay

mv.about: The Maldives is a chain of about 1,200 coral islands grouped in 26 atolls in the Indian Ocean southwest of India and Sri Lanka. With roughly 520,000 people speaking Dhivehi, it is Asia's smallest country by area and population, and the lowest-lying nation on Earth, averaging about 1.5 metres above sea level. A Buddhist kingdom converted to Islam in 1153, it became a British protectorate in 1887 and gained independence in 1965, becoming a republic in 1968. Its economy depends on luxury tourism and fishing, and rising seas pose an existential threat that makes it a leading voice on climate change.

ml.about: Mali is a large, landlocked country in West Africa, stretching from the Sahara in the north to the Niger River savannas in the south. Its about 23 million people speak French officially and Bambara widely, and most are Muslim. The medieval Mali Empire, whose ruler Mansa Musa was famed for his gold, and the later Songhai Empire made Timbuktu a legendary centre of trade and learning. Colonised by France as French Sudan, Mali became independent in 1960. Since 2012 it has been destabilised by Tuareg and jihadist insurgencies in the north and a series of military coups, and is now under junta rule.
dates: Tuareg and jihadist rebellion in the north
known: Music: Ali Farka Touré, Salif Keita

mt.about: Malta is a small archipelago in the central Mediterranean, south of Sicily, with about 540,000 people packed onto three inhabited islands, making it one of the most densely populated countries in the world. Maltese, a Semitic language written in Latin script, and English are both official, and it is a parliamentary republic. Its megalithic temples are older than the pyramids. Held in turn by Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs, Normans and Spain, it was given to the Knights of St John in 1530, who held off the Ottomans in the Great Siege of 1565. Napoleon seized it in 1798, Britain took over soon after, and independence came in 1964.
dates: Knights of St John granted Malta

mh.about: The Marshall Islands is a nation of 29 low-lying coral atolls and five islands scattered across the central Pacific, roughly halfway between Hawaii and Australia. Its about 40,000 people speak Marshallese and English, and the country is a presidential republic. Settled by Micronesians thousands of years ago, the islands were claimed by Germany, taken by Japan in 1914 and seized by the United States in 1944. From 1946 to 1958 the US tested 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak atolls. The country became independent in 1986 under a Compact of Free Association with the US, which still provides most of its budget and defence.
dates: US nuclear testing begins at Bikini
Independence in free association with US

mr.about: Mauritania is a large, mostly desert country in northwest Africa, where the Sahara meets the Atlantic, bordering Western Sahara, Algeria, Mali and Senegal. Its about 5 million people are nearly all Muslim and speak Arabic and various African languages, with French widely used. It is a presidential republic that has seen several military coups. The region was home to the Berber Almoravid movement in the eleventh century and the old caravan towns of Chinguetti and Ouadane. France ruled it from the early 1900s until independence in 1960. It was the last country to abolish slavery, in 1981, and the practice persists; iron ore and fishing drive the economy.
known: Iron ore trains, the world's longest

mu.about: Mauritius is a small volcanic island nation in the Indian Ocean about 2,000 kilometres off the southeast coast of Africa, east of Madagascar. Its about 1.3 million people are mainly of Indian, African, Chinese and French descent; English is the official language but French and Mauritian Creole dominate daily life. It is a parliamentary republic and one of Africa's most stable democracies. Uninhabited until the Dutch arrived in 1598, it was settled by the French, who imported enslaved Africans for sugar plantations, and then taken by Britain in 1810, which brought Indian indentured labourers. Independent since 1968, it has prospered on sugar, textiles, tourism and finance.
dates: Dutch land and name the island

mx.about: Mexico is a large country in southern North America, stretching from the United States border to Guatemala and Belize between the Pacific and the Gulf of Mexico. It has about 130 million people, making it the world's largest Spanish-speaking nation, and is a federal presidential republic. It was the heartland of the Olmec, Maya and Aztec civilisations before Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire in 1521, founding New Spain. Independence came in 1821, followed by the loss of half its territory to the US in 1848 and a decade of revolution after 1910. Today it is a major manufacturing economy with deep cultural influence, but struggles with drug cartel violence.
dates: Loses northern territories to the US
known: Aztec and Maya ruins: Chichén Itzá, Teotihuacan

fm.about: The Federated States of Micronesia is a nation of more than 600 islands spread across the western Pacific north of Papua New Guinea, grouped into four states: Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae. Its about 110,000 people speak English and several local languages, and it is a federal republic. The islands were ruled in turn by Spain, Germany and Japan, and after heavy fighting in World War II became part of a US-administered UN trust territory. The country became independent in 1986 under a Compact of Free Association that leaves defence to the United States and provides much of its income, alongside fishing and subsistence farming.
dates: Spain sells the islands to Germany
Independence in free association with US

md.about: Moldova is a small, landlocked country in eastern Europe between Romania and Ukraine. It has about 2.5 million people, most speaking Romanian, and is a parliamentary republic and one of Europe's poorest countries. Historically the eastern part of the principality of Moldavia, the territory, known as Bessarabia, was annexed by Russia in 1812, joined Romania after 1918, and was seized by the Soviet Union in 1940. Independent since 1991, it has been split since a 1992 war by the breakaway region of Transnistria, which is backed by Russian troops. Moldova is now pursuing EU membership while balancing ties with Russia.

mc.about: Monaco is a tiny city-state on the French Riviera, enclosed by France and the Mediterranean, and the second-smallest country in the world after Vatican City. Its about 39,000 residents, most of them wealthy foreigners, make it the most densely populated nation on Earth; French is official. It is a constitutional monarchy ruled by the Grimaldi family, who seized the rock in 1297 and have held it almost continuously since. Nearly bankrupt in the nineteenth century, it reinvented itself with the Monte Carlo casino in the 1860s and later as a tax haven and playground of the rich, famed for its Grand Prix and glamour.

mn.about: Mongolia is a vast, landlocked country in East Asia sandwiched between Russia and China. With about 3.4 million people over 1.5 million square kilometres, it is the most sparsely populated sovereign state in the world; about half live in the capital. The language is Mongolian, written today in Cyrillic, and the country is a parliamentary republic. In 1206 Genghis Khan united the steppe tribes and launched the largest contiguous land empire in history. The region fell under Qing Chinese rule in the 1690s, declared independence in 1911, and became a Soviet-aligned communist state in 1924 until a peaceful democratic revolution in 1990. Mining and herding dominate the economy.
known: Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire
Naadam festival: wrestling, archery, horse racing

me.about: Montenegro is a small, mountainous country on the Adriatic coast of southeastern Europe, bordered by Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, Kosovo and Albania. It has about 620,000 people, speaking Montenegrin and Serbian, and is a parliamentary republic. Its name, 'Black Mountain', dates from the Venetian era. It survived as a semi-independent principality under prince-bishops during centuries of Ottoman rule and was recognised as independent in 1878. After World War I it was absorbed into Yugoslavia and remained joined with Serbia after that state's breakup. In 2006 it voted narrowly for independence; it joined NATO in 2017 and is negotiating EU membership.
dates: Independence recognised at Congress of Berlin
known: Uses the euro without EU membership

ms.about: Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory in the Leeward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, a small volcanic island of about 4,500 people who speak English. Settled by Irish Catholics in 1632, which earned it the nickname 'Emerald Isle of the Caribbean', it had a plantation economy worked by enslaved Africans. In 1995 the long-dormant Soufrière Hills volcano erupted, burying the capital Plymouth under ash and forcing two-thirds of the population to leave; the southern half of the island remains an exclusion zone. Plymouth is still the official capital, though government operates from Brades in the north.
known: Irish heritage and St Patrick's festival

ma.about: Morocco sits at the northwest corner of Africa, facing Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar, with coasts on both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean and the Atlas Mountains running through its interior. It has about 37 million people, speaking Arabic and Berber (Amazigh) officially with French widely used, and is a constitutional monarchy whose king holds extensive power. Berber dynasties such as the Almoravids and Almohads built empires spanning Spain and North Africa, and the current Alaouite dynasty has ruled since the 1600s. A French and Spanish protectorate from 1912, it regained independence in 1956. It controls most of Western Sahara, whose status remains disputed.
dates: Idrisid dynasty founds the first Moroccan state

mz.about: Mozambique is a long country on the southeast coast of Africa, facing Madagascar across the Mozambique Channel and bordering South Africa, Zimbabwe, Malawi and Tanzania among others. It has about 33 million people, with Portuguese the official language alongside many Bantu languages, and is a presidential republic. Swahili and Arab traders worked its coast for centuries before Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498 and Portugal made it a colony. Independence in 1975 after a liberation war was followed by a devastating civil war until 1992. It has large natural gas reserves but remains poor, and faces a jihadist insurgency in the north.
dates: Vasco da Gama lands on the coast
Civil war between FRELIMO and RENAMO begins
Islamist insurgency begins in Cabo Delgado
known: Indian Ocean beaches and Bazaruto Archipelago
Island of Mozambique, old Portuguese capital

mm.about: Myanmar, also known as Burma, is the largest country in mainland Southeast Asia, lying between India, Bangladesh, China, Laos and Thailand on the Bay of Bengal. Its about 55 million people are mostly Buddhist Burmese speakers, alongside many ethnic minorities, several of which have fought long insurgencies. The Pagan kingdom built thousands of temples at Bagan from the eleventh century, and later Burmese kingdoms were conquered by Britain in three wars. Independent in 1948, it fell under military rule in 1962. A fragile democratic opening under Aung San Suu Kyi ended with a coup in 2021, plunging the country into civil war.

na.about: Namibia is a large, sparsely populated country on the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa, bordered by Angola, Botswana and South Africa. Its about 2.6 million people live mostly in the north; English is official, with Oshiwambo, Afrikaans and German widely spoken, and it is a presidential republic. The Namib, the world's oldest desert, runs the length of its coast. Germany colonised it in 1884 and committed genocide against the Herero and Nama in 1904 to 1908. South Africa seized it in 1915 and ruled it under apartheid until a long guerrilla war led by SWAPO brought independence in 1990. Mining, especially diamonds and uranium, drives the economy.

nr.about: Nauru is a single raised coral island of 21 square kilometres in the central Pacific, the world's smallest island nation and third-smallest country overall, with about 12,000 people speaking Nauruan and English. It is a parliamentary republic with no official capital; government offices sit in Yaren district. Annexed by Germany in 1888 and administered by Australia after 1914, it was mined for phosphate from bird droppings, which made Nauruans briefly among the richest people per head in the world after independence in 1968. The phosphate ran out, the wealth was squandered, and the island now depends on Australian aid and hosting an offshore immigration detention centre.
dates: Japanese occupation in World War II

np.about: Nepal is a landlocked country in the Himalayas, wedged between India and China's Tibet, and home to eight of the world's ten highest mountains including Everest. Its about 30 million people speak Nepali and dozens of other languages, and most are Hindu, with a significant Buddhist minority; the Buddha was born at Lumbini in the south. The Gorkha king Prithvi Narayan Shah unified the kingdom in 1768, and it was never colonised, though it fell within Britain's sphere. A Maoist civil war from 1996 to 2006 and a royal massacre in 2001 led to the monarchy's abolition in 2008, when Nepal became a federal republic.
known: Birthplace of the Buddha at Lumbini

nl.about: The Netherlands is a small, flat, densely populated country on the North Sea coast of western Europe, bordered by Germany and Belgium, with about a quarter of its land lying below sea level. It has about 18 million people speaking Dutch and is a constitutional monarchy; Amsterdam is the capital but government sits in The Hague. The Dutch won independence from Spain in an eighty-year war and in the seventeenth century built a global trading empire, producing Rembrandt and Vermeer. Occupied by Germany in World War II, it became a founding member of the EU and is known for its liberal social policies.
dates: Eighty Years' War against Spain begins
Independence recognised at Peace of Westphalia
known: Dykes and land reclaimed from sea

nc.about: New Caledonia is a French overseas territory in the southwest Pacific, about 1,200 kilometres east of Australia, consisting of the large main island Grande Terre and smaller islands. Its about 270,000 people are divided between the indigenous Kanak people, descendants of European settlers and other groups, and speak French. France annexed it in 1853 and used it as a penal colony; it holds about a quarter of the world's nickel reserves. Tension between Kanak independence supporters and loyalists erupted into violence in the 1980s and again in 2024. It has a special autonomous status within France, and three referendums between 2018 and 2021 rejected independence.
dates: James Cook sights and names the island
known: World's largest lagoon and barrier reef

nz.about: New Zealand is an island country in the southwest Pacific, about 2,000 kilometres southeast of Australia, made up of the North and South Islands and many smaller ones. Its about 5.3 million people speak English, with Māori and sign language also official, and it is a parliamentary democracy under the British monarch. The Māori arrived from Polynesia around 1300, making it the last major landmass settled by humans. The 1840 Treaty of Waitangi between Māori chiefs and the British Crown founded the colony. It became a dominion in 1907 and was the first country to grant women the vote. Its economy rests on farming, tourism and its spectacular scenery.
dates: First country to give women the vote
known: All Blacks rugby and the haka
Lord of the Rings film locations

ni.about: Nicaragua is the largest country in Central America, lying between Honduras and Costa Rica with coasts on both the Pacific and the Caribbean, and containing Lake Nicaragua, the region's biggest lake. Its about 7 million people speak Spanish, and it is a presidential republic that has become increasingly authoritarian. Colonised by Spain in the 1520s, it gained independence in 1821 and endured US intervention and the long Somoza dictatorship, which the Sandinista revolution overthrew in 1979. The 1980s brought a US-backed Contra war. Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega returned to power in 2007 and has since crushed opposition, leaving one of the region's poorest countries.

ne.about: Niger is a large, landlocked country in West Africa, more than three-quarters covered by the Sahara, lying north of Nigeria and bordering Algeria, Libya, Chad, Mali and Burkina Faso. Its about 27 million people, mostly Hausa and Zarma and nearly all Muslim, speak French officially, and it has the world's highest birth rate and one of its lowest development rankings. Trans-Saharan trade passed through Agadez, and the territory came under French rule in the early 1900s. Independent since 1960, it has suffered repeated coups, most recently in 2023, when the military ousted the elected president and expelled French and American forces. Uranium is its main export.

ng.about: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, with about 220 million people, on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa between Benin and Cameroon. English is the official language among over 500 others, chiefly Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo; the north is mainly Muslim and the south mainly Christian. It is a federal presidential republic. Ancient Nok, Benin and Yoruba cultures and the northern Hausa and Sokoto states preceded British colonial rule, consolidated in 1914. Independent in 1960, it suffered the Biafran civil war and decades of military rule before democracy returned in 1999. Oil wealth, Nollywood and Afrobeats make it an African powerhouse, though poverty and insecurity persist.
dates: Britain unites northern and southern protectorates
known: Oil production in the Niger Delta

nu.about: Niue is a single raised coral island in the South Pacific, about 2,400 kilometres northeast of New Zealand, with a population of only about 1,700, making it one of the least populated places with self-government. Its people speak Niuean and English and are New Zealand citizens; many more Niueans live in New Zealand than on the island. A British protectorate from 1900 and then annexed to New Zealand, it has been a self-governing state in free association with New Zealand since 1974, which handles its defence and foreign affairs. Known as 'the Rock of Polynesia', it offers limestone caves, whale watching and clear waters.
dates: James Cook visits, calls it 'Savage Island'
Self-government in free association with NZ
known: Tiny population, more Niueans in NZ

nf.about: Norfolk Island is a small Australian external territory in the Pacific, about 1,400 kilometres east of mainland Australia, with about 2,000 people. Discovered by James Cook in 1774, it served as a brutal British penal colony in two periods before 1855. In 1856 the descendants of the Bounty mutineers were resettled here from Pitcairn Island, and many islanders still trace their ancestry to them and speak Norfuk, a blend of English and Tahitian. The island had its own legislative assembly from 1979 until Australia abolished it in 2015 and integrated the territory into its mainland laws, a move still resented by many residents.
dates: Pitcairn Islanders resettled from Bounty mutineers

kp.about: North Korea occupies the northern half of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia, bordering China and briefly Russia, with South Korea across the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone. Its about 26 million people speak Korean and live under one of the world's most closed and repressive regimes, a hereditary communist dictatorship ruled by the Kim family since 1948. Korea was a Japanese colony from 1910 until 1945, when it was divided between Soviet and American zones. The 1950 to 1953 Korean War ended in stalemate, not peace. Famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands, and the state has since built nuclear weapons despite international sanctions.
dates: DPRK founded under Kim Il Sung
Kim Jong Il succeeds his father

mk.about: North Macedonia is a small, landlocked country in the central Balkans, bordered by Serbia, Kosovo, Bulgaria, Greece and Albania. Its about 1.8 million people are mostly Macedonian speakers, with a large Albanian minority, and it is a parliamentary republic. The region was the heart of the ancient Macedonian kingdom of Philip II and Alexander the Great, later ruled by Rome, Byzantium, Serbia and five centuries of Ottoman control. It became a Yugoslav republic in 1944 and declared independence peacefully in 1991. A long dispute with Greece over the name 'Macedonia' was settled in 2018 when it added 'North', opening the way to NATO membership in 2020.
dates: Albanian insurgency ends with Ohrid Agreement
known: Lake Ohrid, one of Europe's oldest lakes

mp.about: The Northern Mariana Islands are a US commonwealth of 14 islands in the western Pacific, north of Guam and east of the Philippines, with about 50,000 people, most on Saipan. English, Chamorro and Carolinian are official, and residents are US citizens who do not vote for president. Spain claimed the islands in the 1500s, sold them to Germany in 1899, and Japan took them in 1914. Saipan and Tinian saw ferocious battles in 1944, and the atomic bomb missions launched from Tinian. The islands became a UN trust territory under the US and chose commonwealth status in 1975. Tourism dominates the economy.
dates: Spain sells the islands to Germany
known: Battle of Saipan and WWII sites

no.about: Norway occupies the western and northern part of the Scandinavian peninsula, with a long coastline of deep fjords on the North Sea and Arctic Ocean, stretching far above the Arctic Circle and including the Svalbard archipelago. Its about 5.5 million people speak Norwegian, and it is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system and one of the world's highest standards of living. Viking seafarers raided and settled across Europe from the 790s. Norway was united with Denmark for four centuries and then with Sweden until peaceful independence in 1905. Oil discovered in the North Sea in 1969 built an enormous sovereign wealth fund; Norway has twice rejected EU membership.
dates: Kalmar Union with Denmark and Sweden

om.about: Oman lies on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, facing the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman, with a strategic exclave on the Strait of Hormuz; it borders the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Yemen. Its about 4.6 million people, including many foreign workers, speak Arabic and mostly follow Ibadi Islam, a branch distinct from Sunni and Shia. It is an absolute monarchy under a sultan. A maritime empire in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, it controlled Zanzibar and parts of the East African coast. Sultan Qaboos, who deposed his father in 1970, modernised a deeply isolated country during a fifty-year reign and made Oman a trusted regional mediator.
dates: Qaboos deposes his father, begins modernisation
known: Desert forts and Muscat's Grand Mosque
Wadis, dunes and the Hajar Mountains

pk.about: Pakistan lies in South Asia between India, Afghanistan, Iran and China, with a coast on the Arabian Sea and the Karakoram mountains, including K2, in the north. Its about 240 million people make it the fifth most populous country; Urdu and English are official, with Punjabi the most spoken, and nearly all are Muslim. It is a federal parliamentary republic in which the army wields great influence. Home to the ancient Indus Valley civilisation, the region was part of British India until partition in 1947 created Pakistan as a homeland for Muslims. It has fought several wars with India, lost East Pakistan as Bangladesh in 1971, and has nuclear weapons.
dates: Return to civilian rule after Musharraf

pw.about: Palau is a nation of about 340 islands in the western Pacific, east of the Philippines, with roughly 18,000 people speaking Palauan and English. It is a presidential republic. Spain, Germany and Japan ruled the islands in turn, and Peleliu was the site of one of the bloodiest Pacific battles of World War II. After the war it joined the US-administered trust territory and in 1994 became its last part to gain independence, under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, which handles its defence. The capital moved from Koror to purpose-built Ngerulmud in 2006. Palau is a pioneer of marine conservation.
dates: Independence in free association with US

ps.about: Palestine comprises the West Bank and the Gaza Strip in the eastern Mediterranean Levant, home to about 5 million mostly Arabic-speaking people. The State of Palestine is recognised by most UN members and has been a UN observer state since 2012, though it is not a full member. The Palestinian Authority administers parts of the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, while Gaza has been run by Hamas since 2007. Palestinians claim East Jerusalem as their capital; Ramallah serves as the administrative centre. Its status, borders and statehood remain the core of the unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
dates: Israel occupies West Bank and Gaza
known: Dome of the Rock in East Jerusalem

pa.about: Panama is the narrow isthmus joining Central and South America, with coasts on both the Caribbean and the Pacific. About 4.4 million people live in this Spanish-speaking presidential republic, whose economy is built on the canal, banking, shipping registries and the US dollar. A Spanish colony, it became part of Colombia after independence in 1821, then separated in 1903 with US backing so the canal could be built. The United States ran the Canal Zone until handing it over in 1999, a decade after invading to remove the dictator Manuel Noriega.
dates: Independence from Spain, joins Gran Colombia

pg.about: Papua New Guinea occupies the eastern half of New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, plus hundreds of smaller islands north of Australia. Its roughly 10 million people, most living in rural villages, speak over 800 languages, the most of any country; English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu are official. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. Divided between Germany and Britain in the 1880s, then administered by Australia, it saw fierce fighting in the Second World War and became independent in 1975. A long separatist war on Bougainville ended in the late 1990s.
dates: Germany and Britain claim the territory
known: Birds of paradise and highland tribes

py.about: Paraguay is a landlocked country in the heart of South America, wedged between Argentina, Brazil and Bolivia, with the Paraguay River dividing the fertile east from the dry Chaco. About 7 million people live in this presidential republic, and most are bilingual in Spanish and Guaraní, the indigenous language that is unusually widely spoken. Independent since 1811, it was devastated by the War of the Triple Alliance in the 1860s, fought Bolivia over the Chaco in the 1930s, and endured Alfredo Stroessner's 35-year dictatorship until a 1989 coup opened the way to democracy.
dates: War of the Triple Alliance begins

pe.about: Peru lies on South America's Pacific coast, stretching from desert shoreline over the Andes into the Amazon basin. About 34 million people live in this presidential republic, speaking Spanish along with Quechua and Aymara. It was the centre of the Inca Empire until Francisco Pizarro's conquest in the 1530s, then the richest Spanish viceroyalty, before independence in 1821. The twentieth century brought military rule, the Shining Path insurgency of the 1980s and Alberto Fujimori's authoritarian decade; recent years have seen rapid growth alongside chronic political turmoil.

ph.about: The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands in Southeast Asia, home to about 115 million people. Filipino and English are official, and it is Asia's largest predominantly Catholic nation, a legacy of three centuries as a Spanish colony from 1565. Ceded to the United States in 1898, occupied by Japan in the Second World War, it became independent in 1946. Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law until the 1986 People Power Revolution restored democracy. It is a presidential republic with a large diaspora of overseas workers.

pn.about: The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory in the remote South Pacific, halfway between New Zealand and Peru. Only Pitcairn itself is inhabited, by around 50 people, making it the least populous jurisdiction in the world. The islanders descend from the mutineers of HMS Bounty and their Tahitian companions, who settled there in 1790 to hide from the Royal Navy. English and the Pitkern creole are spoken. The territory is administered from New Zealand by a British governor, and its waters form one of the largest marine reserves on earth.

pl.about: Poland is a large Central European country on the Baltic Sea, with about 38 million Polish-speaking people and a parliamentary republic. A kingdom from the tenth century, it formed the vast Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569, was wiped off the map by partitions in 1795, and reappeared in 1918. The Nazi and Soviet invasion of 1939 began a brutal occupation; after the war Poland became a Soviet-bloc communist state. The Solidarity movement led by Lech Wałęsa helped end communism in 1989, and Poland joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004.

pt.about: Portugal occupies the western edge of the Iberian Peninsula along the Atlantic, together with the Azores and Madeira islands. About 10.5 million people speak Portuguese in this semi-presidential republic. A kingdom since 1143, it led the Age of Discovery in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries and built an empire from Brazil to Macau. Lisbon was levelled by an earthquake in 1755; the monarchy fell in 1910 and the Salazar dictatorship followed until the peaceful Carnation Revolution of 1974, after which Portugal shed its colonies and joined the European Community in 1986.
known: Port wine and pastéis de nata

pr.about: Puerto Rico is an unincorporated territory of the United States in the northeastern Caribbean, with about 3.2 million mostly Spanish-speaking residents. Puerto Ricans have been US citizens since 1917, yet cannot vote for president and have no voting member of Congress; the island has its own elected governor and legislature under a 1952 constitution. Settled by Spain from 1508, it was ceded to the United States after the Spanish-American War of 1898. Debates over statehood, independence or continued commonwealth status recur, and Hurricane Maria in 2017 caused lasting damage.

qa.about: Qatar is a small peninsula jutting into the Persian Gulf from the Arabian mainland, bordering only Saudi Arabia. Its roughly 3 million residents are mostly foreign workers; citizens number a few hundred thousand. Arabic-speaking and ruled as an absolute monarchy by the Al Thani family, it was a British protectorate until independence in 1971. Vast natural gas reserves have made it one of the richest countries per capita, funding the Al Jazeera network, a global airline and the 2022 World Cup. A Saudi-led blockade isolated it from 2017 to 2021.
known: Doha skyline and Museum of Islamic Art

cg.about: The Republic of the Congo, often called Congo-Brazzaville, sits on the Atlantic coast of Central Africa, facing its larger namesake across the Congo River. About 6 million people live there, speaking French, Lingala and Kituba, with most concentrated in Brazzaville and the port of Pointe-Noire. A French colony within French Equatorial Africa, it gained independence in 1960, declared itself a Marxist people's republic in 1969, and has been dominated by Denis Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979 to 1992 and again since a 1997 civil war. Oil drives the economy.
dates: Brazza signs treaty with local ruler
Civil war returns Sassou Nguesso to power
known: Brazzaville facing Kinshasa across the river

ro.about: Romania lies in southeastern Europe, where the Carpathian Mountains curve through the country and the Danube reaches the Black Sea. About 19 million people speak Romanian, a Romance language descended from Roman settlers in ancient Dacia. It is a semi-presidential republic and member of NATO and the EU. The principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859, independence from the Ottomans came in 1878, and Transylvania was added in 1918. Communist rule after 1947 culminated in Nicolae Ceaușescu's dictatorship, overthrown in a violent revolution in December 1989.

ru.about: Russia is the largest country on earth, spanning eleven time zones from the Baltic to the Pacific across Eastern Europe and northern Asia. About 144 million people, mostly Russian-speaking, live under a federal presidential system dominated by Vladimir Putin since 2000. The state grew from medieval Kievan Rus and Muscovy into the tsarist empire, was transformed by the 1917 Revolution into the Soviet Union, bore the brunt of defeating Nazi Germany, and was a superpower until the USSR collapsed in 1991. Its 2022 invasion of Ukraine has left it isolated from the West.
dates: Peter the Great founds St Petersburg

rw.about: Rwanda is a small, densely populated, landlocked country in East Africa's Great Lakes region, known as the land of a thousand hills. About 14 million people speak Kinyarwanda, with English, French and Swahili also official. Colonised by Germany and then Belgium, it became independent in 1962 amid Hutu-Tutsi tensions that exploded in the 1994 genocide, when some 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu were killed in about a hundred days. Under President Paul Kagame, in power since 2000, it has rebuilt into one of Africa's most orderly and fast-growing states, though with tight political control.
known: Mountain gorillas in Volcanoes National Park

bl.about: Saint Barthélemy, or St Barts, is a tiny French island in the Leeward Islands of the Caribbean with about 10,000 residents. It is an overseas collectivity of France, having separated administratively from Guadeloupe in 2007, and uses the euro. France first settled it in 1648, then ceded it to Sweden in 1784; the capital Gustavia still bears the name of the Swedish king, and the island returned to France in 1878. Dry and short of fresh water, it has become one of the world's most exclusive resorts, drawing yachts and celebrities.

sh.about: Saint Helena is a rugged volcanic island in the South Atlantic, about 2,000 kilometres from Africa, and one of the most remote inhabited places on earth. Around 4,000 English-speaking islanders, known as Saints, live in this British Overseas Territory, which also governs Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Discovered by the Portuguese in 1502 and settled by the East India Company in 1659, it is best known as the place of Napoleon's final exile from 1815 until his death in 1821. An airport finally opened in 2017 after centuries of access only by ship.

kn.about: Saint Kitts and Nevis is a two-island federation in the Leeward Islands of the eastern Caribbean. With about 48,000 people, it is the smallest sovereign state in the Americas by both area and population. English is spoken, and it is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. Saint Kitts was England's first Caribbean colony in 1623 and became a sugar powerhouse worked by enslaved Africans; Britain's hold was confirmed in 1783. Independence came in 1983. Nevis narrowly voted against secession in 1998, and the country pioneered citizenship-by-investment schemes.
dates: First English colony in the Caribbean

lc.about: Saint Lucia is a mountainous volcanic island in the Windward Islands of the eastern Caribbean, home to about 180,000 people. English is official and a French-based creole is widely spoken, reflecting a colonial past in which the island changed hands between France and Britain fourteen times before Britain prevailed in 1814. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm, independent since 1979, with an economy based on tourism and bananas. Remarkably for its size, it has produced two Nobel laureates, the economist Arthur Lewis and the poet Derek Walcott.

mf.about: Saint Martin is the French northern part of a small Caribbean island shared with Dutch Sint Maarten, the smallest inhabited island in the world divided between two countries. About 32,000 people live in this French overseas collectivity, which split administratively from Guadeloupe in 2007 and uses the euro. The island was partitioned by the Treaty of Concordia in 1648, and the open border has held ever since. Tourism dominates, with beaches, duty-free shopping and a reputation for fine dining. Hurricane Irma caused enormous destruction in 2017.
dates: Island divided between France and Netherlands
known: Island shared with Dutch Sint Maarten

pm.about: Saint Pierre and Miquelon is a small French archipelago just south of Newfoundland, the last remnant of France's North American empire. Its roughly 6,000 inhabitants speak French, use the euro and live in a French overseas collectivity. Claimed by France in the sixteenth century, the islands were repeatedly contested with Britain before being confirmed as French in the early 1800s. Cod fishing sustained them for centuries, and during US Prohibition they boomed as a base for liquor smuggling. A 1992 ruling limited their fishing zone, hurting the economy.
dates: Returned to France after loss of Canada
known: Last French foothold in North America

vc.about: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines consists of the volcanic main island of Saint Vincent and a chain of smaller Grenadine islands in the eastern Caribbean, with about 110,000 English-speaking people. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. Indigenous Caribs and the mixed-ancestry Garifuna resisted European settlement fiercely; after Britain took control the Garifuna were deported in 1797. Independence came in 1979, the year La Soufrière volcano erupted, as it did again in 2021. Bananas and tourism, especially sailing among the Grenadines, support the economy.
known: Sailing the Grenadines, Bequia and Mustique

ws.about: Samoa is a Polynesian nation of two main islands, Upolu and Savai'i, in the South Pacific, with about 220,000 people who speak Samoan and English. It is a parliamentary democracy in which only chiefly titleholders, or matai, may stand for parliament, blending Westminster rules with the traditional fa'a Samoa way of life. Germany took the western islands in 1900, New Zealand seized them in 1914, and in 1962 Samoa became the first Pacific island state to regain independence. In 2011 it jumped westward across the International Date Line to align with Australia and New Zealand.
known: Fa'a Samoa and matai chief system

sm.about: San Marino is a microstate of 61 square kilometres entirely surrounded by Italy, perched on Mount Titano near the Adriatic coast. About 34,000 Italian-speaking people live in what claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, founded by tradition in 301 AD by the stonemason Saint Marinus. It is governed by two Captains Regent elected every six months, an arrangement dating to the Middle Ages. Protected by Italy and sharing its currency, it survived Italian unification intact and even had Western Europe's first freely elected communist-led government from 1945 to 1957.
known: Captains Regent elected twice a year

st.about: São Tomé and Príncipe is a two-island nation in the Gulf of Guinea off Central Africa, and the continent's second-smallest country, with about 230,000 Portuguese-speaking people. Uninhabited until Portuguese settlers arrived in the 1490s, the islands became sugar and later cocoa plantations worked by enslaved and contract labourers; by the early 1900s they were the world's top cocoa producer. Independence came in 1975 as a one-party socialist state, and multiparty democracy followed in 1991. It is a semi-presidential republic with a small economy based on cocoa, tourism and aid.

sa.about: Saudi Arabia covers most of the Arabian Peninsula, a land of deserts including the vast Rub' al Khali. About 36 million people, a third of them foreign workers, live under an absolute monarchy ruled by the House of Saud with Islamic law. As guardian of Mecca and Medina, Islam's holiest cities, it hosts millions of pilgrims each year. The kingdom was forged in 1932 by Ibn Saud, and the discovery of oil in 1938 made it a global energy power. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has pushed sweeping social and economic reforms since 2017.
dates: Mohammed bin Salman becomes crown prince

sn.about: Senegal is the westernmost country of mainland Africa, on the Atlantic coast at the edge of the Sahel. About 18 million people live in this presidential republic; French is official and Wolof the common tongue, and Islam predominates. France founded Saint-Louis in 1659 and made Dakar the capital of French West Africa. Independent since 1960 under the poet-president Léopold Senghor, Senegal is one of Africa's most stable democracies, with peaceful transfers of power in 2000, 2012 and 2024. Gorée Island near Dakar is a memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.
dates: First peaceful change of ruling party

rs.about: Serbia is a landlocked country in the central Balkans, with about 6.6 million Serbian-speaking, mostly Orthodox people. A parliamentary republic and EU candidate, it maintains close ties with Russia. A powerful medieval kingdom fell to the Ottomans in the fifteenth century; independence was recognised in 1878, and in 1918 Serbia became the core of Yugoslavia. The federation's bloody breakup in the 1990s, the Kosovo war and NATO's 1999 bombing left deep scars. Montenegro left the union in 2006, and Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not recognise.
dates: Battle of Kosovo against the Ottomans

sc.about: The Seychelles are an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean off East Africa, with about 100,000 people, the smallest population of any African country. Seychellois Creole, English and French are official. Uninhabited until the French settled in 1770, the islands passed to Britain in 1814 and became independent in 1976. A coup the next year brought France-Albert René's one-party rule until multiparty politics returned in 1993. Tourism and tuna have given it Africa's highest income per person, and nearly half its land area is protected as nature reserves.

sl.about: Sierra Leone lies on West Africa's Atlantic coast, with about 8.5 million people who speak English officially and Krio as a common language. It is a presidential republic. Freetown was founded in the late 1700s by British abolitionists as a home for freed slaves, and the colony became a hub of West African education. Independent since 1961, the country suffered a devastating civil war from 1991 to 2002, fuelled by diamond wealth, followed by the 2014 Ebola epidemic. It remains poor but has held several peaceful elections since the war.
known: Diamonds and the blood diamond trade

sg.about: Singapore is a city-state on an island at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, with about 6 million people packed into 730 square kilometres. English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil are official, reflecting its Chinese, Malay and Indian mix. Founded as a British trading post by Stamford Raffles in 1819, it fell to Japan in 1942, joined Malaysia in 1963 and was expelled into independence in 1965. Under Lee Kuan Yew and the People's Action Party, which has governed continuously, it became one of the world's richest and most orderly states, a global port and financial hub.
known: Marina Bay Sands and Gardens by the Bay

sx.about: Sint Maarten is the Dutch southern part of a small Caribbean island shared with French Saint Martin, and one of the four constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. About 45,000 people live there, speaking Dutch and English. The island was divided by the Treaty of Concordia in 1648, and Sint Maarten was part of the Netherlands Antilles until that federation dissolved in 2010, when it gained its own government under the Dutch crown. Tourism dominates, with cruise ships, casinos and the famous beach beside the airport runway. Hurricane Irma caused severe damage in 2017.
dates: Island divided between Netherlands and France
known: Shared island with French Saint Martin

sk.about: Slovakia is a landlocked Central European country of about 5.4 million Slovak-speaking people, with the Tatra Mountains in the north and the Danube in the south. A parliamentary republic, it joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and the eurozone in 2009. Slovak lands were part of the Kingdom of Hungary for nearly a thousand years before joining the Czechs in Czechoslovakia in 1918. A Nazi-aligned Slovak state existed during the Second World War, followed by communist rule until the 1989 Velvet Revolution. The peaceful Velvet Divorce from the Czech Republic created independent Slovakia in 1993.
known: World's top car production per capita

si.about: Slovenia is a small Central European country of about 2.1 million Slovene-speaking people, stretching from the Julian Alps to a short Adriatic coastline. A parliamentary republic, it joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and the euro in 2007, the first former Yugoslav republic to do so. Slovene lands were under Habsburg rule for centuries before joining the new Yugoslav kingdom in 1918 and Tito's socialist federation after 1945. It declared independence in 1991 and secured it after a brief Ten-Day War, escaping the worse conflicts that followed elsewhere in Yugoslavia.
known: Mount Triglav and the Julian Alps

sb.about: The Solomon Islands are a Melanesian nation of hundreds of islands east of Papua New Guinea, with about 750,000 people speaking more than 70 languages; English is official and Pijin the lingua franca. It is a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. A British protectorate from 1893, it saw the pivotal Battle of Guadalcanal in the Second World War and became independent in 1978. Ethnic violence around 2000 prompted an Australian-led intervention that lasted until 2017. In 2019 it switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China, and a 2022 security pact with Beijing drew wide attention.
dates: Spanish explorer Mendaña names the islands
Switches recognition from Taiwan to China

so.about: Somalia occupies the Horn of Africa, with the longest coastline on the African mainland, and about 18 million mostly Somali-speaking Muslim people. Formed in 1960 by merging British and Italian Somaliland, it was ruled by Siad Barre from 1969 until his fall in 1991 plunged the country into clan warfare and state collapse. Since 2012 a federal government in Mogadishu has slowly rebuilt, still fighting the al-Shabaab insurgency. Somaliland in the northwest has run itself as a de facto independent state since 1991 but is not internationally recognised. Piracy off its coast peaked around 2010.
dates: Independence and union of two Somalilands
Battle of Mogadishu, Black Hawk Down
known: Piracy off the Horn of Africa

za.about: South Africa occupies the southern tip of the continent, with about 62 million people and twelve official languages including Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and English. A parliamentary republic, it spreads government across three capitals: Pretoria for the executive, Cape Town for parliament and Bloemfontein for the courts. Dutch settlers arrived in 1652, Britain later took the Cape, and the Boer War of 1899 to 1902 preceded union in 1910. The apartheid system of racial segregation imposed in 1948 ended with Nelson Mandela's release in 1990 and the first democratic election in 1994. It is Africa's most industrialised economy.

kr.about: South Korea occupies the southern half of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia, with about 52 million Korean-speaking people, half of them in the Seoul metropolitan area. It is a presidential republic and a technological and cultural powerhouse. The Joseon dynasty ruled a unified Korea for five centuries until Japan annexed it in 1910. Liberation in 1945 brought division at the 38th parallel, then the Korean War of 1950 to 1953, which ended in an armistice rather than peace. Decades of authoritarian rule and breakneck industrialisation gave way to democracy in 1987 and today's prosperity.
known: Films like Parasite and Squid Game

ss.about: South Sudan is a landlocked country in east-central Africa and the world's newest sovereign state, independent since 2011. About 11 million people live there; English is official, and Dinka and Nuer are the largest of many ethnic groups, mostly Christian or following traditional beliefs. It separated from Sudan after two long civil wars, in 1955 to 1972 and 1983 to 2005, and an overwhelming referendum vote. A presidential republic led by Salva Kiir since independence, it collapsed into its own civil war in 2013; a 2018 peace deal holds uneasily. Oil provides nearly all revenue, yet poverty is severe.
known: Sudd wetland on the White Nile

es.about: Spain covers most of the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe, plus the Balearic and Canary Islands and two enclaves in North Africa. About 48 million people live in this parliamentary monarchy of 17 autonomous regions; Spanish is national, with Catalan, Basque and Galician co-official regionally. Roman and Visigothic rule gave way to Muslim al-Andalus from 711 until the Reconquista ended in 1492, the year Columbus sailed and a global empire began. Decline, civil war in the 1930s and Franco's dictatorship until 1975 were followed by a swift transition to democracy and EU membership in 1986.

lk.about: Sri Lanka is a teardrop-shaped island off the southern tip of India, home to about 22 million people who speak mainly Sinhala and Tamil. It is a presidential republic; the legislative capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, a suburb of the commercial hub Colombo. Buddhist Sinhalese kingdoms flourished from antiquity at Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa before Portuguese, Dutch and finally British rule. Independent as Ceylon in 1948, the country endured a 26-year civil war with Tamil Tiger separatists and a severe economic crisis in 2022.
dates: British take Kandy, control whole island
Civil war ends with Tamil Tigers defeated

sd.about: Sudan lies in northeast Africa, where the Blue and White Nile meet at Khartoum. About 48 million people live there, speaking Arabic and many local languages. Ancient Nubia and the Kingdom of Kush rivalled Egypt, leaving more pyramids than Egypt itself. After Anglo-Egyptian rule, Sudan became independent in 1956 but suffered decades of civil war, which led to South Sudan breaking away in 2011. Dictator Omar al-Bashir was ousted in 2019; a 2021 coup and then a devastating war between the army and the RSF militia since 2023 have shattered the country.
dates: War between army and RSF begins
known: Confluence of the Blue and White Nile

sr.about: Suriname, on the northern coast of South America, is the continent's smallest sovereign country and its only Dutch-speaking one, with about 600,000 people. Most live near the coast; over 90 percent of the land is rainforest. The Dutch acquired it in 1667, trading New Amsterdam (New York) to England, and ran sugar plantations with enslaved Africans, later bringing Indian and Javanese contract workers, which explains today's remarkably mixed population. Independent since 1975, it endured a 1980 military coup under Desi Bouterse before returning to democracy. It is a presidential republic.

se.about: Sweden is the largest Nordic country, stretching from the Baltic to the Arctic, with about 10.5 million mostly Swedish-speaking people and a parliamentary constitutional monarchy. Forged as a kingdom under Gustav Vasa in the 1500s, it was a Baltic great power in the 1600s before losing Finland to Russia in 1809. It then stayed out of every war for two centuries, building a famous welfare state and export industries. Sweden joined the EU in 1995 and, abandoning its neutrality after Russia invaded Ukraine, NATO in 2024.
dates: Kalmar Union with Denmark and Norway

ch.about: Switzerland is a landlocked Alpine country of about 9 million people with four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. It is a federal republic of 26 cantons where citizens vote directly on laws several times a year. Born from a 1291 alliance of mountain valleys against the Habsburgs, the confederation grew by adding cantons, had its neutrality recognised at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and became a modern federal state in 1848. Staying out of both world wars, it became one of the richest countries on Earth, known for banking, precision industry and hosting international organisations.
dates: Independence from the Holy Roman Empire recognised
Neutrality guaranteed at Congress of Vienna

sy.about: Syria sits at the eastern end of the Mediterranean, bordering Turkey, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon and Israel. Its roughly 23 million people speak Arabic, with Kurdish and other minorities. Damascus and Aleppo are among the oldest continuously inhabited cities, and Damascus was capital of the Umayyad Caliphate. After four centuries of Ottoman rule and a French mandate, Syria became independent in 1946. The Assad family ruled from 1970 until a brutal civil war that began in 2011 ended with rebels toppling Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, leaving a transitional government to rebuild a shattered country.

tw.about: Taiwan is a mountainous island off China's southeast coast with about 23 million people, mostly Mandarin-speaking, and a vibrant democracy. Ruled by the Dutch, the Qing dynasty and then Japan, it was handed to the Republic of China in 1945; in 1949 the Nationalist government retreated there after losing the Chinese civil war. Decades of martial law gave way to full democracy in the 1990s. Taiwan governs itself under the name Republic of China, but the People's Republic of China claims it, and most countries do not formally recognise it. It is a world leader in semiconductors.

tj.about: Tajikistan is a landlocked, overwhelmingly mountainous country in Central Asia, bordering Afghanistan and China, with about 10 million people. Tajik, a form of Persian, sets it apart from its Turkic-speaking neighbours. Heir to the Samanid empire that made Bukhara a centre of Persian culture, the region was absorbed by Russia in the 1800s and became a Soviet republic. Independence in 1991 was followed by a bloody civil war; Emomali Rahmon has ruled as president since 1992. It is the poorest of the former Soviet states, heavily dependent on remittances from workers in Russia.
dates: Civil war begins; Rahmon takes power

tz.about: Tanzania lies on the East African coast, with about 65 million people united by Swahili alongside English and over a hundred local languages. It is a presidential republic; Dodoma is the official capital while Dar es Salaam is the largest city. The Swahili coast traded with Arabia and India for centuries, and Zanzibar became a sultanate and slave market. Germany colonised the mainland, Britain took over after World War I, and Tanganyika won independence in 1961 under Julius Nyerere, uniting with Zanzibar in 1964. Nyerere's socialist experiment gave way to market reforms and multiparty politics in the 1990s.

th.about: Thailand occupies the heart of mainland Southeast Asia, with about 70 million Thai-speaking people and a constitutional monarchy in which the army has often intervened. Known as Siam until 1939, it is the only Southeast Asian country never colonised, as its kings played Britain and France against each other. The Sukhothai and Ayutthaya kingdoms shaped Thai culture before Bangkok was founded in 1782 under the Chakri dynasty that still reigns. A 1932 revolution ended absolute monarchy, and the country has since swung between elected governments and military coups while becoming a manufacturing and tourism powerhouse.

tl.about: Timor-Leste, or East Timor, occupies the eastern half of Timor island at the end of the Indonesian archipelago, with about 1.3 million mostly Catholic people speaking Tetum and Portuguese. A Portuguese colony for over four centuries, it declared independence in 1975 only to be invaded by Indonesia days later; the occupation cost perhaps a quarter of the population. A 1999 UN-backed referendum chose independence despite militia violence, and after UN administration the country became fully sovereign in 2002, making it Asia's youngest nation. It is a semi-presidential republic reliant on offshore oil and gas.

tg.about: Togo is a narrow strip of West Africa between Ghana and Benin, stretching from a short Atlantic coast to the savanna. About 9 million people speak French plus Ewe, Kabiye and others. A German colony from 1884, it was split between Britain and France after World War I, and French Togo became independent in 1960. Since a 1967 coup the Gnassingbe family has ruled, first Eyadema and since 2005 his son Faure, who in 2024 pushed through a constitution shifting power to a prime minister post he then took. Phosphates and Lome's port drive the economy.
known: Voodoo culture and Lome's fetish market

tk.about: Tokelau is a dependent territory of New Zealand made up of three tiny coral atolls in the South Pacific, north of Samoa, with about 1,500 people speaking Tokelauan and English. There is no airport; the only access is a day-long boat trip from Samoa. A British protectorate from 1889, it was placed under New Zealand administration in 1925. Referendums in 2006 and 2007 on self-government in free association with New Zealand narrowly fell short of the required majority, so it remains a territory, though it runs its own affairs through village councils and a rotating head of government.
known: No airport, reached only by boat
One of the smallest populations on Earth

to.about: Tonga is a Polynesian kingdom of about 170 islands in the South Pacific, with roughly 100,000 people speaking Tongan and English. The medieval Tu'i Tonga empire held sway over much of the region. King George Tupou I unified the islands in 1845 and gave them a constitution in 1875, and Tonga was never colonised, only a British protected state from 1900 to 1970. It remains the Pacific's only monarchy, though reforms in 2010 made most parliament seats elected. In 2022 a huge underwater volcanic eruption and tsunami devastated the islands.

tt.about: Trinidad and Tobago is a two-island republic at the southern end of the Caribbean, just off Venezuela, with about 1.4 million English-speaking people of mainly African and Indian descent. Spanish for three centuries, Trinidad passed to Britain in 1797, and Tobago was joined to it in 1889. Independence came in 1962 and republic status in 1976. Unlike most Caribbean neighbours it is industrial, with oil and natural gas making it one of the region's richest countries. Its Carnival, calypso and the steelpan, the only acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century, are famous worldwide.

tn.about: Tunisia is North Africa's smallest country, wedged between Algeria and Libya on the Mediterranean, with about 12 million Arabic-speaking people; French is widely used. Ancient Carthage, Rome's great rival, stood near today's capital Tunis. Arab conquest, Ottoman rule and a French protectorate from 1881 followed. Independent in 1956 under Habib Bourguiba, it became one of the Arab world's most secular and educated societies. In 2011 the Jasmine Revolution overthrew Ben Ali and sparked the Arab Spring; Tunisia built a democracy that President Kais Saied has steadily rolled back since 2021.
known: Sahara and Star Wars film sets

tr.about: Turkey bridges Europe and Asia, with Istanbul straddling the Bosphorus and the capital Ankara in the Anatolian heartland. About 85 million people speak Turkish, with a large Kurdish minority. Anatolia hosted Hittites, Greeks, Romans and Byzantines before Turkic Seljuks arrived in 1071; the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and built an empire spanning three continents. After defeat in World War I, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk founded a secular republic in 1923. A NATO member since 1952 and long-time EU candidate, Turkey became a presidential republic under Recep Tayyip Erdogan in 2017.

tm.about: Turkmenistan lies in Central Asia between the Caspian Sea, Iran and Uzbekistan, mostly covered by the Karakum desert. Its roughly 7 million people speak Turkmen. The Silk Road city of Merv was once among the world's largest. Russia conquered the region in the 1880s, and it became a Soviet republic before independence in 1991. Since then it has been one of the most closed and authoritarian states on Earth, ruled by the eccentric Saparmurat Niyazov and then the Berdimuhamedow family, who have built a white-marble capital on revenues from some of the world's largest natural gas reserves.
dates: Russian conquest completed at Geok Tepe
known: Darvaza gas crater, the Gates of Hell

tc.about: The Turks and Caicos Islands are a British Overseas Territory in the Atlantic, southeast of the Bahamas, with about 45,000 people, mostly English-speaking. The capital Cockburn Town is on Grand Turk, while Providenciales holds most of the population and the resorts. Bermudian salt rakers settled the islands in the 1680s; they were later governed from the Bahamas and then Jamaica before becoming a separate colony in 1962. Britain imposed direct rule from 2009 to 2012 after a corruption scandal. Tourism built on some of the world's finest beaches, plus offshore finance, drives the economy.

tv.about: Tuvalu is a Polynesian nation of nine low-lying coral atolls in the central Pacific, with about 11,000 people speaking Tuvaluan and English. It is a parliamentary democracy with the British monarch as head of state. Formerly the Ellice Islands, it was ruled by Britain jointly with the Gilbert Islands before separating in 1975 and gaining independence in 1978. With its highest point only a few metres above sea level, Tuvalu has become a symbol of the threat of rising seas; in 2023 it signed a treaty with Australia offering its citizens a path to migrate.
dates: Part of Gilbert and Ellice Islands colony
known: One of the world's smallest countries

ug.about: Uganda is a landlocked country on the East African plateau, bordering Lake Victoria, with about 48 million people speaking English, Swahili and many local languages, Luganda chief among them. The powerful Buganda kingdom became a British protectorate in 1894, and Uganda gained independence in 1962. Idi Amin's brutal dictatorship in the 1970s and civil war followed, until Yoweri Museveni took power in 1986; he has ruled ever since. Fertile and green, Uganda was called the Pearl of Africa by Churchill, and holds the source of the Nile and half of the world's mountain gorillas.
known: Source of the Nile at Jinja

ua.about: Ukraine is the largest country entirely in Europe, stretching from the Carpathians to the Black Sea, with about 38 million Ukrainian-speaking people before millions fled the war. Kyiv was the heart of medieval Kyivan Rus. Later divided between Poland, Austria and Russia, it endured Soviet rule and the Holodomor famine before independence in 1991. Pro-Western revolutions in 2004 and 2014 were answered by Russia seizing Crimea and backing separatists in the east, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022 that Ukraine continues to resist. It is a semi-presidential republic and a candidate for EU membership.

ae.about: The United Arab Emirates is a federation of seven emirates on the Arabian Peninsula's Gulf coast, led by Abu Dhabi and the glittering commercial hub Dubai. Of about 10 million residents, almost 90 percent are foreign workers; Arabic is official and English ubiquitous. Known as the Trucial States under British protection from the 1800s, the sheikhdoms united in 1971 as Britain withdrew. Oil discovered in the 1950s turned a land of pearl divers into one of the richest per capita on Earth. Hereditary rulers govern each emirate, with the ruler of Abu Dhabi serving as president.
dates: Burj Khalifa opens as tallest building
Abraham Accords normalise ties with Israel
known: Emirates airline and global trade hub

gb.about: The United Kingdom unites England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland on islands off northwest Europe, with about 68 million people and a parliamentary constitutional monarchy, one of the world's oldest. English kings and parliament fought out the balance of power over centuries, with Magna Carta and the 1688 revolution setting precedents for liberty. The union with Scotland in 1707 created Great Britain, which launched the Industrial Revolution and ruled the largest empire in history. After leading the fight in two world wars, it dismantled the empire, built the NHS welfare state and in 2020 left the European Union.
known: Big Ben and the Tower of London

us.about: The United States spans North America from Atlantic to Pacific, plus Alaska and Hawaii, with about 335 million people, mostly English-speaking, and the world's largest economy and military. Thirteen British colonies declared independence in 1776 and adopted a federal constitution in 1787 that still governs. The nation expanded westward, abolished slavery after a bloody civil war, absorbed waves of immigrants and became an industrial giant. Victory in World War II and the Cold War made it the dominant superpower. It is a federal presidential republic of 50 states whose politics are sharply divided between Democrats and Republicans.
dates: Emerges from World War II as superpower

vi.about: The United States Virgin Islands are an unincorporated territory of the United States in the eastern Caribbean, east of Puerto Rico, with about 87,000 mainly English-speaking people on St Thomas, St John and St Croix. Denmark colonised the islands from the 1670s and ran sugar plantations with enslaved labour until emancipation in 1848. Fearing Germany might seize them, the US bought the islands from Denmark in 1917 for 25 million dollars. Residents are US citizens but cannot vote for president. The capital Charlotte Amalie on St Thomas is one of the Caribbean's busiest cruise ports.
dates: United States buys islands from Denmark
known: Virgin Islands National Park on St John

uy.about: Uruguay is a small, flat country of rolling grassland on South America's Atlantic coast, squeezed between Argentina and Brazil, with about 3.4 million Spanish-speaking people, nearly half in Montevideo. Long contested by Spain, Portugal, Argentina and Brazil, it became an independent buffer state in 1828. In the early 1900s it pioneered welfare and secular reforms, earning the nickname Switzerland of South America. A military dictatorship from 1973 to 1985 gave way to one of the region's most stable democracies, notable for legalising cannabis in 2013. It is a presidential republic built on beef, wool and soy.
dates: Hosts and wins first World Cup
known: Football and the first World Cup

uz.about: Uzbekistan is the most populous country in Central Asia, with about 36 million Uzbek-speaking people, and one of only two doubly landlocked countries on Earth. Its oasis cities Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva were jewels of the Silk Road, and Timur made Samarkand the capital of his vast empire in the 1300s. Russia conquered the region in the 1800s; under Soviet rule cotton monoculture drained the Aral Sea. Independent since 1991, it was ruled harshly by Islam Karimov until 2016, after which Shavkat Mirziyoyev loosened controls. It remains a presidential republic with limited political freedom.
known: Silk Road cities of Bukhara and Khiva

vu.about: Vanuatu is a Y-shaped chain of about 80 volcanic islands in the southwest Pacific, with roughly 330,000 Melanesian people who speak over a hundred languages, united by the creole Bislama alongside English and French. Known as the New Hebrides, it was ruled jointly and awkwardly by Britain and France as a condominium from 1906 until independence in 1980. It is a parliamentary republic. Subsistence farming, tourism and the sale of citizenship support the economy, and the islands are among the world's most exposed to cyclones, earthquakes and volcanoes.
dates: Cook names the islands New Hebrides
known: Pentecost land diving, origin of bungee
Mount Yasur, an accessible active volcano
Diving the SS President Coolidge wreck
World's highest linguistic diversity per capita

va.about: Vatican City is the world's smallest state, a walled enclave of 44 hectares inside Rome with about 800 residents. It is an absolute monarchy ruled by the Pope, elected for life by the cardinals, and serves as the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church. Popes governed a broad swath of central Italy as the Papal States from the 700s until Italian unification seized Rome in 1870. The 1929 Lateran Treaty with Mussolini's Italy created today's sovereign state. Italian and Latin are the working languages, and the Swiss Guard has protected the Pope since 1506.
dates: Italy captures Rome, ending Papal States
Leo XIV elected first American pope

ve.about: Venezuela lies on South America's Caribbean coast, with about 29 million Spanish-speaking people and the world's largest proven oil reserves. Simon Bolivar, born in Caracas, led its independence from Spain and founded Gran Colombia, from which Venezuela split in 1830. Oil made it South America's richest country by the mid-1900s, with a stable democracy after 1958. Hugo Chavez's socialist Bolivarian Revolution from 1999 and Nicolas Maduro's rule since 2013 brought economic collapse, hyperinflation and the emigration of over 7 million people. Maduro's claimed victory in the 2024 election was widely disputed.

vn.about: Vietnam curves along the eastern edge of mainland Southeast Asia, from the Red River delta around Hanoi to the Mekong delta in the south, with about 100 million Vietnamese-speaking people under a one-party communist state. A thousand years of Chinese rule ended in 938, followed by independent dynasties. France colonised it in the 1800s; Ho Chi Minh declared independence in 1945 and defeated the French at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. The country was partitioned, and the Vietnam War ended with the communist north's victory in 1975. Market reforms since 1986 have made it a booming manufacturing economy.
dates: Independence from China at Bach Dang
French defeated at Dien Bien Phu
Fall of Saigon ends Vietnam War

wf.about: Wallis and Futuna is a French overseas collectivity in the South Pacific between Fiji and Samoa, made up of Wallis island and the Futuna and Alofi islands, with about 11,000 people. French is official alongside Wallisian and Futunan, Polynesian languages. Unusually, three traditional kingdoms, Uvea, Sigave and Alo, survive within the French system, and their kings sit on the territorial council. French Catholic missionaries arrived in 1837 and converted the islands; France made them a protectorate in the 1880s and an overseas territory after a 1959 vote. Many islanders live in New Caledonia.

eh.about: Western Sahara is a sparsely populated desert territory on Africa's Atlantic coast between Morocco and Mauritania, with about 600,000 people, mostly Arabic-speaking. A Spanish colony from 1884, it was abandoned by Spain in 1975 and claimed by Morocco, which marched 350,000 settlers in; the Sahrawi independence movement Polisario proclaimed a republic and fought Morocco until a 1991 UN ceasefire. Morocco now administers about 80 percent, including Laayoune and the phosphate mines, behind a long sand wall, while Polisario holds the interior and runs refugee camps in Algeria. A promised UN referendum has never been held.

ye.about: Yemen occupies the southwest corner of the Arabian Peninsula, with about 34 million Arabic-speaking people. Ancient Saba, linked to the Queen of Sheba, grew rich on incense, and Mocha gave coffee to the world. Britain held Aden from 1839 while the Ottomans and then imams ruled the north; a republic emerged in the north in 1962 and a Marxist state in the south in 1967, uniting in 1990. A 2011 uprising ousted Ali Abdullah Saleh, and since Houthi rebels seized Sana'a in 2014 a civil war with Saudi intervention has caused one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

zm.about: Zambia is a landlocked country on the high plateau of south-central Africa, with about 20 million people speaking English and some 70 local languages, led by Bemba and Nyanja. Named for the Zambezi river, it was Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company and then Britain, which exploited the Copperbelt. Kenneth Kaunda led it to independence in 1964 and ran a one-party state until multiparty elections in 1991. Copper still dominates the economy. It is a presidential republic that has seen several peaceful transfers of power, including Hakainde Hichilema's 2021 victory.

zw.about: Zimbabwe is a landlocked country in southern Africa between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, with about 16 million people speaking Shona, Ndebele and English. The stone city of Great Zimbabwe, which gives the country its name, was a medieval trading capital. Cecil Rhodes's company colonised it as Southern Rhodesia in 1890; in 1965 the white minority declared independence from Britain, leading to a guerrilla war. Majority rule came in 1980 under Robert Mugabe, whose 37-year rule brought violent land seizures and hyperinflation before the army ousted him in 2017. It is a presidential republic.
